ideas.name: State air-emission event reports (TCEQ, LDEQ) as a unit-trip detector for refineries, crackers, chlor-alkali, fertilizer and gas plants
ideas.sector_focus: Energy and materials: refiners, commodity chemicals, fertilizer, gas processing, Permian E&P flaring, Texas EAF steel
ideas.mechanism: Texas (TCEQ Air Emission Event Reports) and Louisiana (LDEQ EDMS) require operators to report unplanned emission events within 24 hours, naming the site, the unit (FCCU, cracker, cell line, compressor), start and end time, event type and cause. Counting unplanned event-hours and unit-shutdown events at a company's named sites gives a quarterly unplanned-downtime index per company, which maps to lost throughput for refiners (Delek Tyler/Big Spring, PBF Chalmette, Calumet Shreveport), lost production for chemical makers (Westlake, Olin Freeport, Huntsman Port Neches, LyondellBasell Channelview, Eastman Longview, Celanese Clear Lake, Orion, Cabot, Kronos, Chemours Ingleside), fertilizer (CF Donaldsonville, Mosaic Louisiana), gas processors (Kinetik) and Permian E&P flaring. The gap is between disclosed planned turnarounds and the unplanned downtime visible in filings before the company reports volumes.
ideas.measurement_window: Event level, full quarter; initial reports within 24 hours and final reports within about two weeks, so the quarter's index is final ~14 days after quarter end; companies report 25-45 days after quarter end.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3%: roughly 35-40 names with major Texas or Louisiana process plants: refiners DK, PBF, CLMT; chemicals WLK, OLN, HUN, LYB, EMN, CE, CC, KRO, OEC, CBT; fertilizer CF, MOS; midstream KNTK, WES, PAA; LNG VG (if under the cap); steel STLD (Sinton), CMC (Seguin); E&Ps PR, MTDR, SM, CIVI, VTLE, HPK. Not covered: CVI, DINO, PARR (no TX/LA plants).

Chemical, fertilizer, gas-plant and E&P events are much less covered; consensus for small chemical names rarely reflects a two-week cracker outage until the company says so (REASONED). Priced in: headline refinery outages mostly; smaller chemical-plant downtime little.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: IIR Energy (industrial outage database) and Wood Mackenzie/Genscape refinery monitoring (REASONED; not on the named list). None from the named list.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free, event-level, 24-hour lag, extended beyond refining to chemicals, fertilizer, gas processing and E&P flaring where no outage desk looks, and measured as company-level unplanned event-hours per quarter rather than headline refinery outages.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: An increase of more than one standard deviation in a company's unplanned event-hours at its TX and LA sites in a quarter versus its trailing 8-quarter mean, measured 14 days after quarter end (~20 days before the release), predicts negative revenue and EBITDA surprises and a negative close T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus XLE/XLB, controlling for consensus revisions, crack and ethylene spread moves, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Refineries and crackers run at 90-95% utilization, so an unplanned trip of a cracker or FCCU costs days of output plus a restart, and the margin lost per day is large when spreads are wide. Small events such as opacity exceedances are noise; unit shutdowns longer than 24 hours are the signal.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Event counts correlate weakly with lost production (many events are flaring during restarts); large outages are pre-announced or picked up by trade press and are already in estimates; site-to-company mapping errors; the Delek 2026 count of one record shows per-company samples can be too thin.

ideas.name: EPA NPDES discharge-monitoring-report effluent flow and organic load as a throughput nowcast for single-site process plants
ideas.sector_focus: Materials and energy: single- or few-site chemicals, nitrogen fertilizer, pulp and paper, specialty cellulose, refining
ideas.mechanism: Every NPDES permittee must submit monthly discharge monitoring reports to EPA/state systems with flow (parameter 50050) and pollutant loads (BOD, TOC, ammonia) per outfall, and EPA ECHO exposes them per permit through a keyless REST endpoint. For a process plant, discharge volume and organic/ammonia load scale with production throughput, so YoY change in monthly-average flow and load over the quarter nowcasts volumes at that plant. For companies whose revenue comes from one or two US plants (AdvanSix Hopewell, LSB Industries' three ammonia plants, CVR Partners' two, specialty pulp mills), the plant nowcast is a company nowcast; the gap versus consensus volume assumptions is the edge.
ideas.measurement_window: Months 1-2 of the quarter are available 3-4 weeks before early-November earnings; month 3 arrives about 6 weeks after month end. TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: the AdvanSix Hopewell permit (VA0005291) effluent chart showed Flow monthly-average values for the monitoring period ending 30-SEP-26, so the lag was about 6 weeks. Some parameters on this permit appear bimonthly or quarterly rather than monthly (TESTED HERE pattern), so the window varies by permit.

ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A YoY change of at least 10% in the monthly-average effluent flow (parameter 50050) summed across a plant's process outfalls over months 1-2 of the quarter, measured at least 14 days before the earnings release, predicts a same-direction volume/revenue surprise versus final consensus and a same-direction close T-1 to close T+1 abnormal return versus XLB, controlling for the relevant BLS PPI change, consensus revisions, size and momentum.

ideas.name: Great Lakes iron-ore loadings by port (Lake Carriers' Association) as a Cleveland-Cliffs mine and blast-furnace nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Materials and shipping: integrated steel and taconite mining on the Great Lakes
ideas.mechanism: LCA publishes monthly iron-ore shipments by loading port within 2-3 days of month end. Port-to-mine mapping is nearly one-to-one: Silver Bay = Northshore (CLF), Marquette = Tilden (CLF), Two Harbors = Minntac (Nippon/US Steel), Duluth and Superior = United Taconite, Minorca, Hibbing (CLF-majority) and Keetac (REASONED). Cliffs' pellets mostly feed its own blast furnaces (Burns Harbor, Indiana Harbor, Cleveland, Middletown, Dearborn), so loadings at CLF ports track pellet production (mine costs, idlings) and the furnaces' planned run-rate, hence steel shipments and fixed-cost absorption in the quarter being reported. A year-over-year drop concentrated at CLF ports while non-CLF ports are flat is the edge versus consensus volume assumptions.
ideas.measurement_window: Monthly by port; the quarter's final month is posted ~3 days after month end (TESTED HERE: the October 2026 report was posted 2026-11-03); CLF reports ~20-25 days after quarter end. January-March is the lock-closure season so Q1 reads are mostly inventory draws.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.1%: Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF) is the only US-listed name with a direct mapping; Algoma Steel (ASTL, NASDAQ, small, an ore buyer) is peripheral.

ideas.name: FAA aircraft-registry diffs as a Textron Aviation (and Bell) delivery nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Industrials: business-jet, turboprop and helicopter OEMs
ideas.mechanism: Every aircraft delivered to a US customer receives an N-number registration with manufacturer, model, serial, year of manufacture, registrant type and certificate-issue date, and the FAA publishes the entire registry nightly. Diffing nightly snapshots and counting new Textron Aviation serials (Citation 525/525B/525C, 560XL, 680A, 700 jets; 208B and 408 turboprops; 172/182/206 pistons) and Bell helicopters, excluding entries registered to the manufacturer itself (inventory and demonstrators) and tracking 'registration pending' rows, gives a running count of US deliveries by model during the quarter. Textron discloses jet and turboprop deliveries each quarter and the stock trades on them; the US share of Citation deliveries is roughly 65-75% (REASONED from this session's 2026 counts versus recent annual delivery rates), so the scaled count predicts the delivery number and Aviation-segment revenue.
ideas.measurement_window: Nightly snapshots; the quarter's count is final ~3-7 days after quarter end allowing for certificate-issue lag and pending entries (REASONED); Textron reports ~22-25 days after quarter end.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.4%: Textron (TXT) is the primary name; Embraer ADR (ERJ, Phenom/Praetor) only if ADRs are allowed; aircraft lessors (AL, WLFC, FTAI) weakly since most lessees register abroad; Bristow (BRS) as a helicopter buyer is marginal.

ideas.name: ADS-B airborne-callsign census for regional, ULCC and cargo-charter operators as a block-hour and completion nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Regional airlines under capacity purchase agreements, ultra-low-cost carriers, cargo and charter operators
ideas.mechanism: SkyWest is paid per completed block hour and departure under capacity purchase agreements with incentives tied to completion factor; Sun Country's cargo segment is paid per block hour flying freighters and its charter segment per flight; ULCC revenue is departures x seats x load x fare. Counting distinct airborne callsigns by ICAO prefix (SKW, SCX, AAY, FFT, JBU, ASA/QXE, and cargo ATN/ABX/GTI) at fixed times each day is a direct physical count of completed flying, including unscheduled cargo and charter flying that schedule databases omit; summed over the quarter it nowcasts block hours and completion factor. TESTED HERE: one anonymous OpenSky call over CONUS at 08:28 UTC returned 664 airborne aircraft with JBU 24, ASA 13, FFT 11, SCX 7, ATN 6, ABX 6, GTI 5 (overnight sample, regionals absent).
ideas.target: revenue (block hours, departures); EPS surprise via completion-factor incentives
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter, sampled several times per day; final reading on the last day of the quarter, 3-5 weeks before the release.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1%: SKYW, SNCY, ALGT, ULCC, JBLU, ALK (mainline ASA plus Horizon QXE); cargo operators are mostly private or acquired (Atlas, ATSG - REASONED), helicopter operator VTOL has poor over-water coverage. About 6-8 names.

ideas.vendors_selling_similar: FlightAware (AeroAPI/Firehose), Cirium, OAG, Flightradar24 sell flight tracking and schedule data (these vendors exist; whether any packages block-hour nowcasts for investors is UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free continuous census instead of five-figure data licences, granular to callsign prefix so it captures cargo and charter flying absent from schedules, and tied to each operator's block-hour revenue model.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A shortfall of at least 3% in quarter-to-date distinct daily SKW callsigns (or SCX cargo tails) versus the run-rate implied by the company's last block-hour guidance, measured 5 days before the SKYW or SNCY release, predicts a negative revenue surprise and a negative T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus JETS/IYT, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Regional carriers and cargo operators are paid for flying completed, not for seats sold, so block hours and completion factor are the revenue line. Every airliner broadcasts its position and callsign over ADS-B, which volunteer receiver networks aggregate and publish for free.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Anonymous ADS-B coverage has gaps and the callsign count is not block hours (stage length varies), airlines pre-disclose capacity and traffic monthly or at conferences, and block-hour guidance variance for SKYW is small; OpenSky's free tier is non-commercial by its terms, which is a legal flag for a fund.

ideas.name: Taiwan dedicated-OEM monthly revenue as a sell-in nowcast for US branded golf, bicycle, apparel and footwear mid-caps
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer discretionary: golf equipment, bicycle/suspension components, performance apparel and footwear brands that outsource manufacturing to Taiwan-listed contract manufacturers
ideas.mechanism: Taiwan-listed companies must publish prior-month revenue by the 10th of each month, and several are near-single-category suppliers to US brands: Fusheng Precision (6670, golf club heads) and Advanced International Multitech (8938, TPEx, carbon shafts/heads) supply Callaway, Titleist and TaylorMade; Giant (9921) and Merida (9914) are the largest bicycle OEMs and buy suspension from Fox Factory; Eclat (1476) supplies performance garments to Lululemon, Nike and Under Armour; Pou Chen (9904) is the largest athletic-footwear OEM. The supplier's shipment revenue is the brand's wholesale cost-of-goods sell-in roughly 1-2 months before the brand recognizes wholesale revenue, so the full quarter's supplier revenue is known by the 10th of the month after quarter-end, 2-5 weeks before the US brand reports. A gap between the mapped suppliers' 3-month YoY growth and the consensus-implied revenue growth for the brand is the signal. Applies to brands with a dominant wholesale/sell-in model and a Taiwan supplier whose revenue is concentrated in that category (REASONED; supplier-customer pairs from the brands' 10-K supplier disclosures and the Taiwan firms' annual reports).
ideas.measurement_window: All three months of the brand's fiscal quarter when the brand reports 25-45 days after quarter-end (Acushnet, Topgolf Callaway, Fox Factory, Columbia, Crocs); for FY-offset brands reporting 20-25 days after quarter-end (Deckers, Under Armour) months 1-2 are certain and month 3 arrives 10-15 days before the release.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2-3%: 25-35 names. Likely fits (REASONED; verify caps): Acushnet (GOLF), Topgolf Callaway (MODG), Fox Factory (FOXF), Deckers (DECK), Crocs (CROX), Columbia (COLM), Under Armour (UAA), Wolverine (WWW), Steve Madden (SHOO).

ideas.who_already_knows: Taiwan sell-side covers every one of these suppliers and some US consumer analysts cite Eclat for Lululemon/Nike and Fusheng/AIM for golf (REASONED). Bloomberg and FactSet carry the monthly series. For the largest pairs (Nike, Lululemon) it is likely priced within days; for mid-caps with 5-12 analysts (Acushnet, Fox Factory, Wolverine) the month-3 print is rarely folded into consensus before the release (REASONED). The edge is the gap between the supplier-implied growth and consensus, not the level.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: No vendor known to sell Taiwan monthly revenue mapped to US mid-cap brand pairs at scale (UNKNOWN). Bloomberg/FactSet distribute the raw monthly series.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free, same-day, and pair-mapped to options-listed mid-caps; the gap is computed against consensus-implied growth rather than used as a level.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A positive (negative) gap of at least 10 percentage points between the revenue-weighted 3-month YoY growth of a brand's mapped Taiwan suppliers and the consensus-implied YoY revenue growth for the same fiscal quarter, measured 15-25 days before the brand's earnings release, predicts a positive (negative) close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus XLY and a same-sign revenue surprise, controlling for 30-day consensus revisions, sector, size and 12-1 momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Branded sporting-goods and apparel companies own design and marketing but outsource nearly all manufacturing to Asian contract manufacturers, many of them listed in Taiwan, where exchange rules force monthly revenue disclosure. The supplier's shipments are the brand's inventory purchases, so they lead the brand's wholesale revenue by the shipping-and-recognition lag.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Most suppliers serve several brands (Pou Chen is dominated by Nike and Adidas; Giant sells its own brand), so pair-level attribution is noisy; TWD/USD moves and FOB versus landed timing blur the mapping; and the brand's quarter can be driven by DTC sell-through and discounting rather than sell-in, so supplier revenue can rise while the brand's margin falls. For the best-known pairs the data is already in sell-side notes.

ideas.name: Taiwan monthly-revenue chain map: TWSE/TPEx open-data prints of Taiwanese peers, customers and distributors as a three-month nowcast for US mid-cap semis and hardware
ideas.sector_focus: Semiconductors, semiconductor equipment and test, electronic components, optical/AI-server hardware
ideas.mechanism: Taiwan-listed companies must publish prior-month revenue on MOPS by the 10th of each month, so the full quarter of a Taiwanese firm is public roughly 10 days after quarter end, before most US mid-caps report. For a US company whose revenue is (a) a function of a Taiwanese customer's output (test and assembly equipment sold to OSATs; probe cards consumed per wafer out at TSMC/UMC/Winbond/Nanya), (b) directly competitive with a Taiwanese peer in the same product (SIMO vs Phison 8299 in NAND controllers; HIMX vs Novatek 3034 and Raydium 3592 in display drivers; FormFactor vs MPI 6223 in probe cards; Cohu vs WinWay 6515 in test sockets; Amkor/ChipMOS vs ASE 3711, PTI 6239, KYEC 2449, Chipbond 6147), or (c) sold through Taiwanese distributors (WPG 3702, WT 3036, Supreme 8112 for Diodes, Vishay, Semtech, Power Integrations), a weighted basket of the three monthly prints nowcasts the US company's quarter. AI-connectivity and optical names (Credo, Astera Labs if within the cap band, Fabrinet, Applied Optoelectronics) map to the AI-server ODMs Wiwynn 6669 and Quanta 2382. Data labels: TESTED HERE for the two open-data endpoints; mapping is REASONED from 10-K customer and competitor disclosures.
ideas.measurement_window: Full fiscal quarter: three monthly revenue prints of the mapped Taiwan basket (month 3 published by the 10th of the following month). Interim one- and two-month readings are available 45-75 days before the US print. Most mapped US names report 25-50 days after quarter end, so the final reading leads by 15-35 days.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~6-8%: about 80-100 names in semiconductors, semi equipment/test, components and optical/AI hardware. Examples: Amkor (AMKR), Kulicke & Soffa (KLIC), FormFactor (FORM), Silicon Motion (SIMO), Himax (HIMX), Diodes (DIOD), Cohu (COHU), Fabrinet (FN).

ideas.who_already_knows: Taiwanese brokers publish monthly revenue trackers and US large-cap semi analysts use TSMC/Hon Hai monthly prints; Bloomberg/FactSet carry the series so institutions can see it. For mid-caps the peer/customer basket is rarely constructed, and the information requires a mapping step, the kind of complexity the market has been shown to under-react to (LITERATURE: Cohen and Frazzini 2008, Economic Links and Predictable Returns, Journal of Finance; Cohen and Lou 2012, Complicated Firms, JFE). REASONED: partially priced via sell-side revisions in the last two weeks before the print; the edge is in names with few analysts.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: No alternative-data vendor is known to sell a ticker-mapped Taiwan-basket nowcast (UNKNOWN); the raw monthly series is on Bloomberg/FactSet terminals.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free source, built as per-company weighted baskets for ~80 US mid-caps that terminal users rarely assemble; three-month full-quarter reading available before the print.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A positive gap of more than 5 percentage points between the USD-converted YoY growth of the summed three-month revenue of a US mid-cap's mapped Taiwan peer/customer basket and the consensus-implied YoY revenue growth for that company, measured 10 days before the earnings date, predicts a positive revenue surprise and a positive T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus SMH/XLK, controlling for 30-day consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Taiwan hosts the foundry, OSAT and ODM core of the electronics supply chain, and its exchange rules force every listed company to disclose monthly revenue by the 10th, the fastest public revenue series in the world. US component and equipment makers sell into or compete with these firms, so much of their quarter has effectively been printed in Taipei before it is reported in the US.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Company-level Taiwan revenue mixes many products, so the basket is a noisy proxy; shipment timing and FX differ from US recognition; large-cap read-throughs (TSMC, Hon Hai) move the sector ETF so the relative abnormal return may be small; and sell-side revisions in the final two weeks may already absorb the information.

ideas.name: Package-registry consumption telemetry: PyPI, npm, Docker Hub and Homebrew downloads of vendor agents and SDKs as a usage nowcast for consumption-priced infrastructure software
ideas.sector_focus: Infrastructure software, developer tools, observability, data platforms, communications APIs
ideas.mechanism: Consumption- and seat-priced infrastructure vendors bill for what runs, and what runs is first installed from public registries that publish download counts daily. Agents and SDKs are re-pulled on every deployment and CI run, so weekly downloads of a vendor's primary packages (ddtrace, elastic-apm, confluent-kafka, pymongo, twilio, @braze/web-sdk, amplitude-analytics, python-gitlab, pagerduty, jfrog CLI, okta SDKs, DigitalOcean doctl via Homebrew) track deployment activity, a leading indicator of consumption revenue and net revenue retention. The measured quantity is mirror-filtered weekly downloads aggregated across registries, compared quarter over quarter. Applies to Elastic, Confluent, MongoDB (if within the cap band), GitLab, JFrog, Dynatrace, PagerDuty, Twilio, Braze, Amplitude, DigitalOcean, Fastly, Okta, Progress. Labels: endpoints TESTED HERE in this run and listed in the working file; link to revenue is REASONED.
ideas.measurement_window: Trailing fiscal quarter of weekly downloads (final reading at T-1); the full-quarter reading is complete the day after quarter end, 25-40 days before most prints.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3-4%: about 40-50 names in infrastructure software and developer tools. Examples: Elastic (ESTC), Confluent (CFLT), GitLab (GTLB), JFrog (FROG), Twilio (TWLO), Braze (BRZE), PagerDuty (PD), DigitalOcean (DOCN).

ideas.industry_context: Consumption-priced software charges for hosts, events or API calls, and the client code that generates those charges is distributed through public package registries that expose download counts. Because agents are re-installed on every deployment, download velocity reflects real deployment activity rather than marketing attention.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Downloads are dominated by CI pipelines, mirrors and version-bump re-installs that are uncorrelated with paid usage; open-source community users never pay (Elastic, MongoDB); and the series may simply track the generic developer-activity cycle, a sector factor rather than company-specific revenue.

vet.changes_made: (1) Backtest first, npm only: the npm API has daily history since 2015 for every package, so a full 10-year cross-sectional test costs nothing; PyPI (180 days), Docker Hub (cumulative count, no history) and Homebrew (CLI tools, rolling windows) are dropped from the primary spec. (2) Measure share of registry-wide downloads, not raw QoQ growth, to strip the secular ecosystem trend, holiday weeks and CI-platform outages; registry totals endpoint confirmed (TESTED HERE). (3) Package selection restricted to vendor-owned production SDKs that gate billable usage (twilio, @braze/web-sdk, @pagerduty/pdjs, @elastic/elasticsearch, @confluentinc/kafka-javascript, @okta/okta-auth-js, @amplitude/analytics-browser, @fastly/js-compute, jfrog-cli-v2-jf); third-party clients (gitbeaker, kafkajs) excluded. (4) Crowdedness revised from 4 to 2: TickerTrends sells npm downloads to investors and Apify actors exist. (5) Signal-noise 3 -> 2 and confidence 25 -> 15: no literature links registry downloads to revenue, and downloads are build-time events that count CI pipelines, not usage. (6) Kill rule stated in the hypothesis.
vet.red_team: Downloads are build-time events: an SDK is pulled once per CI run regardless of how much the customer sends through the product, so the series counts pipelines and mirrors, not billable consumption, and open-source users who never pay dominate for Elastic and Confluent. Any QoQ move is mostly the ecosystem cycle (a sector factor already in IGV) plus version-bump artefacts; what is left is a slow secular curve with no quarter-specific information. Expect the npm-only backtest to show no sign agreement beyond chance; keep only because the test is nearly free and fully historical.

ideas.name: FPDS and USAspending funded-obligation flow rolled up to the parent UEI by fiscal quarter as a revenue nowcast for government-services and defense mid-caps
ideas.sector_focus: Industrials and IT services: government-services contractors, defense electronics, engineering and environmental services
ideas.mechanism: Federal contract actions must be reported to FPDS within three business days of award (FAR 4.604; REASONED) and USAspending ingests FPDS nightly, so obligation dollars by recipient (new awards plus funding modifications on existing IDIQ task orders) are nearly complete for a quarter within 1-2 weeks of quarter-end. For services contractors that recognize revenue as costs are incurred against funded task orders, quarterly funded obligations lead revenue by zero to two quarters and directly drive book-to-bill, which is the guidance metric these companies are judged on. A quarter-end shortfall caused by a continuing resolution or shutdown (the October-November 2025 lapse) or de-obligations and terminations for convenience shows up in FPDS before the contractor reports. This deepens seed 16 by replacing award-level anecdotes with a parent-UEI roll-up of federal_action_obligation by federal fiscal quarter, calibrated against each company's historical revenue and backlog. Applies to contractors with at least 60% federal revenue and mostly unclassified work.
ideas.measurement_window: The full fiscal quarter of obligations, complete within 10-14 days after quarter-end; contractors report 25-45 days after quarter-end, so the whole quarter is in hand 2-4 weeks before the release. Classified contracts and subcontract flow are invisible, so coverage is partial for some names.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3%: 35-40 names. Likely fits (REASONED; verify caps): CACI (CACI), SAIC (SAIC), Parsons (PSN), KBR (KBR), V2X (VVX), Maximus (MMS), ICF (ICFI), Tetra Tech (TTEK), Kratos (KTOS), Mercury Systems (MRCY), AeroVironment (AVAV), BWX Technologies (BWXT), Amentum (AMTM), Leonardo DRS (DRS), VSE (VSEC), Curtiss-Wright (CW).

ideas.who_already_knows: Government-services analysts track book-to-bill from company disclosures and some subscribe to Deltek GovWin IQ, Bloomberg Government or HigherGov, which sell federal award and pipeline data (REASONED), so large awards are priced quickly. The quarter-level funded-obligation roll-up against each company's own revenue history, especially in CR and shutdown quarters, is less commonly done by the generalist holders of mid-cap names (REASONED). Moderately priced.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Deltek GovWin IQ, Bloomberg Government, HigherGov (federal award and opportunity data, REASONED).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free and same-day from the primary feeds, focused on funded obligations and de-obligations by parent UEI (not ceiling values or headline awards), calibrated per company, and timed to the 2-4 week gap before earnings.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A decline of at least 15% YoY in a contractor's quarterly funded obligations (sum of federal_action_obligation across its parent UEI hierarchy), measured 14 days before the earnings release, predicts a negative revenue surprise versus consensus, a book-to-bill below 1.0 and negative close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus XLI, controlling for prior-quarter backlog, consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Government-services firms earn revenue by billing hours and costs against task orders that only exist once an agency obligates money to them, and every obligation is a public record within days. Continuing resolutions and shutdowns stop new obligations, which is why these firms' quarters swing with the appropriations calendar.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Obligations are not revenue: multi-year funding, classified work, subcontract flow and recipient-name mismatches make the roll-up noisy; fiscal-year-end flushes dominate seasonality; the companies pre-announce large awards; and paid federal-data vendors already give the best-covered funds a cleaner version.

ideas.name: STB EP 724 weekly rail-service metrics (cars on line by car type, train speed, dwell) as a demand nowcast for railcar lessors and makers
ideas.sector_focus: Railcar lessors and makers: GATX, Trinity, Greenbrier; rail equipment and services.
ideas.mechanism: Class I railroads file weekly service metrics with the Surface Transportation Board under EP 724, and the STB posts a consolidated workbook (TESTED HERE: 502 weekly columns from 2017-03-29 to 2026-11-04 with 'Cars On Line (Count)' by car type - box, covered hopper, gondola, intermodal, multilevel, open hopper, tank, total - plus average train speed, terminal dwell, loaded and empty cars in revenue service by commodity, and carloads by 22 categories). Slower velocity and higher dwell mean shippers need more cars to move the same freight, so lease utilisation and renewal lease rates rise (GATX's Lease Price Index, Trinity's lease fleet) and cars leave storage, lifting new-car orders at Trinity and Greenbrier; the reverse when service improves (REASONED; TRN and GBX management routinely cite velocity as a demand driver). Car-type-level cars-on-line (tank, covered hopper) maps directly onto the lessors' fleet mix.
ideas.target: revenue (renewal lease-rate change, utilisation, orders) and guidance
ideas.measurement_window: The 13 weeks of the quarter; railroads file weekly and the STB workbook is updated with roughly a one-to-two-week lag, so the quarter-end week is available ~10 days after quarter end, three to four weeks before TRN, GATX and GBX report.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.4%: 4-5 names: GATX (~$5B), TRN (~$3B), GBX (~$1.5B); RAIL and FSTR likely below the size floor; Wabtec too large. Caps REASONED.

GATX and Trinity management comment on velocity each quarter, so the direction is partly priced; weekly car-type-level cars-on-line is rarely used in lessor print models (REASONED).
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: FTR and the Railway Supply Institute/ARCI publish railcar order and backlog data (paid or industry; REASONED). None of the brief's listed alt-data vendors.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Weekly, car-type-level and free, available before the lessors print, versus monthly storage counts and quarterly order statistics that arrive later; also measures service quality rather than carloads (seed 6).
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A 3% or larger YoY increase in Class I tank plus covered-hopper cars on line, combined with a 5% or larger decline in system average train speed over the quarter, with the final week available at least 3 trading days before the release, predicts a positive renewal-lease-rate/utilisation and revenue surprise and positive T-1 to T+2 abnormal return vs XLI for GATX, TRN and GBX, controlling for consensus revisions, carload volumes, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Railcar lessors earn from utilisation and lease-rate renewals on fleets of around 100,000 cars; when railroads run slower, each car completes fewer cycles, so shippers lease more cars, and the railroads' own service metrics are filed weekly with the regulator. Railcar makers' orders follow with a lag as cars leave storage.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Velocity is mostly a railroad-operations story that is already discussed on calls; lease rates reset on multi-year contracts so quarterly revenue moves little; cars on line include railroad-owned fleets; carload volume may dominate the lessor outcome; and the relationship inverts when slow service reflects weak demand rather than congestion.

vet.reject_reason: The transmission mechanism is real but far too slow for a 2-10 day earnings trade: GATX's average renewal term is 54 months and its renewal success rate and Lease Price Index move over years, so a quarter's change in cars-on-line or train speed barely touches that quarter's lease revenue, while GATX's quarterly EPS variance is dominated by the timing of remarketing gains and TRN's and GBX's by backlog-scheduled deliveries, none of which the STB data sees. Even a correct read of fleet tightness is already stated by management on the prior call and in the GATX Lease Price Index, so the print surprise is unrelated to the signal.

ideas.name: EIA-860M monthly generator status transitions (planned to under-construction) as a shipment nowcast for solar trackers, eBOS, storage and switchgear
ideas.sector_focus: Electrical equipment: utility-scale solar trackers and eBOS (Nextracker, Array, Shoals), battery storage integrators (Fluence), power-plant switchgear/electrical (Powell), wind blades (TPI).
ideas.mechanism: Form EIA-860M is a mandatory monthly survey; its Planned sheet lists every planned generator with nameplate MW, technology, state, planned operation month/year and a status code P/L/T/U/V/TS (TESTED HERE: September 2026 file has 1,100 planned solar PV, 483 battery, 236 gas combined-cycle and 192 gas CT units; status codes read 'Under construction <=50%', '>50%', 'construction complete, not yet in operation', etc.). Trackers and eBOS ship when mechanical construction starts, so MW entering status U during the quarter nowcasts tracker/eBOS shipments and revenue (recognised on shipment, REASONED); MW moving to V/TS nowcasts storage-integration milestone revenue (FLNC) and switchgear deliveries for gas plants (POWL, REASONED). Month-over-month slippage of planned operation dates flags project delays that cut guidance.
ideas.measurement_window: Months 1-3 of the quarter; month M's file is published in the last week of M+1 (REASONED from EIA's cadence), so months 1-2 arrive 30-60 days before a print and month 3 only ~0-15 days before (sometimes after it; check per event). Each monthly file is a vintage, so point-in-time backtests are natural.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1%: about 8-12 names: NXT (~$10B), ARRY (~$1B), SHLS (~$1B), FLNC (~$1-2B), POWL (~$3B), BE (~$5B+, if classified Industrials), BW (small), AZZ and PLPC (indirect); TPIC likely below the size floor. Caps REASONED.

(4) Timing: month-3 file lands ~24th of the month after quarter end, so lead time is 5 trading days for ARRY/SHLS (second-week reporters) and often negative for NXT; the proposer's 7 days revised to 5 and per-event checking made mandatory. (5) Crowdedness kept at 2 but with the note that PUDL makes the transitions free to everyone and Kayrros sells a faster satellite version; signal-noise 3 -> 2 for survey lag and status jumps.
vet.red_team: EIA-860M is a respondent survey with sporadic updates: projects jump from P to V in a single month or stay in U for years, so the quarter's 'construction starts' is an artefact of when developers answered, not when piles were driven, and the sell-side already uses the same file for installation tracking. Tracker shipments are scheduled by the supplier's contracted backlog and guided a quarter ahead, so the quarter's revenue surprise is mostly recognition timing and margin (steel, tariffs, 45X domestic-content), while the stocks trade on policy headlines (FEOC, ITC safe-harbour) that swamp a 15% change in a noisy MW ratio. With three names and a 3.5-week publication lag, the usable sample is small and the month-3 file sometimes arrives after the print, leaving two months of signal.

ideas.sector_focus: Energy and materials: thermal and metallurgical coal producers
ideas.mechanism: EIA publishes weekly coal production by state with a 5-day lag, MSHA publishes quarterly production per mine, and EIA-923 fuel receipts name the supplying mine (MSHA ID) for each power plant each month. Combining them gives, per producer, (a) a weekly production nowcast weighted by its mines' share of each state and (b) a demand check from EPA CEMS heat input at the plants that buy from those mines. ideas.name: NRC daily power-reactor status: unplanned outage days at owner-mapped nuclear units
ideas.sector_focus: Utilities / merchant power: owners of US nuclear units
ideas.mechanism: The NRC posts every US reactor's percent power at 00:00 each day. Summing (100% minus reported power) x unit MW across the quarter gives lost MWh per unit; applying ownership shares gives each company's nuclear generation shortfall versus the refueling plan it guided. For a merchant owner (Talen's Susquehanna) lost MWh x hedged/realized price is lost revenue plus replacement-power cost that hits EPS directly; for regulated owners (Pinnacle West 29% of Palo Verde, Evergy 47% of Wolf Creek, Ameren 100% of Callaway, TXNM ~10% of Palo Verde) fuel riders mute it to deferred fuel and O&M. The edge is the unplanned extension or trip: guidance embeds the planned outage duration, consensus EPS usually does not move until management comments.
ideas.target: revenue and EPS surprise (merchant owner); margin/O&M (regulated owners)
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter at daily resolution; final reading the day after quarter end; owners report 30-45 days after quarter end. TESTED HERE: 365-day file current to 11/10/2026.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.5%: 5-6 names. Talen (TLN, if still under the $30B cap), Pinnacle West (PNW), Evergy (EVRG), Ameren (AEE), TXNM Energy (TXNM); WEC at the cap edge. CEG, VST, NRG, D, DUK, SO, PEG, ETR, XEL are above $30B.

ideas.sector_focus: Shipping and industrials: inland tank-barge operators, grain and ethanol handlers, fertilizer and aggregates producers that ship by barge

ideas.name: USDA Cold Storage frozen-fry stocks and NASS Potato Stocks processing use as a Lamb Weston volume and price nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer staples: frozen potato processing
ideas.mechanism: USDA's monthly Cold Storage report gives end-of-month stocks of frozen french fries and other frozen potato products; NASS Potato Stocks reports (December to June) give raw potatoes used for processing in the fall-storage states. Industry frozen-fry inventory rising year-over-year while processing use flattens signals oversupply: processors cut run-rates (lower fixed-cost absorption) and discount, the dynamic behind Lamb Weston's 2024-25 margin collapse. With Lamb Weston at roughly 40% of North American frozen-potato capacity (REASONED), the direction of industry stocks versus the prior year, read at its fiscal quarter end, predicts volume and price/mix in the quarter being reported and the tone of guidance.
ideas.measurement_window: End-of-month stocks released about the 22nd-25th of the following month; Lamb Weston's fiscal quarters end in late August, November, February and May and it reports about five weeks later, so the quarter's final-month reading lands 8-30 days before the release depending on the quarter (REASONED from recent report dates); the minimum is used as lead time.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.1%: Lamb Weston (LW) only; McCain, Simplot and Cavendish are private. Weak read-through to restaurant chains' fry costs.

ideas.name: USDA broiler-hatchery placements, weekly federally inspected slaughter and shell-egg price/inventory as protein-processor nowcasts
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer staples: chicken, egg, pork and beef processors
ideas.mechanism: NASS's weekly Broiler Hatchery report (eggs set, chicks placed) leads broiler slaughter by about seven weeks, so placements through week five of a quarter fix industry chicken supply for that quarter; AMS's weekly Actual Slaughter report gives cattle and hog head counts by day; AMS daily and weekly shell-egg reports give price and inventory. Pilgrim's Pride revenue is roughly industry volume times the AMS chicken cutout; Cal-Maine revenue is layer flock times the AMS egg price, with HPAI flock losses driving price; Smithfield, Hormel and Tyson volumes and spreads follow hog and cattle slaughter and cutouts. The edge is the quarterly average of these series versus consensus revenue, which for CALM, VITL and PPC is set by a few analysts who update infrequently.
ideas.measurement_window: Weekly (hatchery on Wednesdays for the prior week; slaughter final about 12 days after the week; egg prices daily); the quarter's reading is final about 12 days after quarter end; PPC reports ~28-30 days and CALM ~30-40 days after its fiscal quarter end.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.5%: Pilgrim's Pride (PPC), Cal-Maine (CALM), Vital Farms (VITL), Hormel (HRL), Smithfield (SFD), Tyson (TSN, near the cap), Seaboard (SEB, thin volume); about 7 names.

ideas.name: Snowpack, streamflow and water-supply forecasts as a hydro-generation and net-power-cost nowcast for Northwest and Mountain utilities
ideas.sector_focus: Utilities: hydro-heavy regulated electrics in the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies
ideas.mechanism: NRCS SNOTEL snow-water-equivalent, USGS streamflow at the gauges above each utility's own dams and NWRFC water-supply forecasts determine the quarter's hydro output at Idaho Power's Hells Canyon complex, Avista's Spokane and Clark Fork plants, Portland General's Clackamas and Deschutes plants and NorthWestern's Missouri and Madison plants. Low hydro means buying replacement power at Mid-C prices; power-cost adjustment mechanisms pass most of this to customers but each company retains a slice (Idaho Power about 5%; Avista, PGE and NorthWestern deadbands then about 10%, REASONED), so a dry quarter lowers EPS by a computable amount that sell-side updates only after management flags it. The signal is forecast-versus-normal generation for the quarter, valued at Mid-C prices and passed through each company's sharing formula.
ideas.measurement_window: Daily SNOTEL and streamflow; NWRFC water-supply forecasts monthly January-June; the quarter's generation is effectively observed by quarter end and reported ~30 days later. Q2 (runoff) and Q3 (summer) matter most; the forward element is the April-September forecast available by early April.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.4%: IDACORP (IDA), Avista (AVA), Portland General (POR), NorthWestern (NWE); TXNM only via purchased power; about 4-5 names.

vet.reject_reason: The content is already in guidance and sell-side models (hydro ranges are re-guided quarterly), the retained EPS exposure after sharing mechanisms is a few cents at most for IDA/AVA/NWE, and only POR (ROE-deadband PCAM) carries meaningful exposure where Mid-C prices rather than inflow drive the surprise; four names and a heavy gauge-to-plant mapping effort for a near-zero expected surprise. Data are reachable and lawful, so this is a mechanism rejection, not a data rejection.

ideas.name: FERC Electric Quarterly Report (EQR) wholesale sales filed 30 days after quarter end as a revenue nowcast for merchant generators and small IPPs
ideas.sector_focus: Utilities / independent power: merchant generators, renewable yieldcos, coal-plant owners, retail energy marketers
ideas.mechanism: Every FERC-jurisdictional public utility and power marketer must file an Electric Quarterly Report within 30 days after quarter end listing each wholesale transaction: MWh, dollars, counterparty, product and delivery point. Summing transaction revenue and volume across a company's filing subsidiaries gives the quarter's wholesale electricity revenue and realized price before the company reports. For merchant and contracted generators whose revenue is mostly wholesale power sales, this is close to a direct read of reported revenue; the gap versus consensus revenue (which is built from forward curves and hedge disclosures) is the edge. Applies to companies with few generating assets and simple structures, not to vertically integrated utilities.
ideas.measurement_window: Full fiscal quarter (EQR covers all transactions in the calendar quarter). EQR deadlines are Apr 30, Jul 31, Oct 31 and Jan 31 (REASONED from FERC Order 2001 rules), so lead time is 3-10 days for companies reporting in the second week after the deadline and zero or negative for companies that report before the EQR deadline (e.g., late-October reporters).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1-2%: about 10-20 names (REASONED, verify caps): Talen Energy, Ormat Technologies, Clearway Energy, Hallador Energy (single Merom plant), XPLR Infrastructure, Genie Energy; plus wholesale marketing affiliates of mid-cap utilities (Otter Tail, Black Hills, IDACORP, Avista, Portland General, TXNM) where off-system sales margins swing quarters. Vistra, NRG and Constellation are above the cap.

ideas.name: MSHA closure orders and quarterly Form 7000-2 hours/tonnage by controller as a production nowcast for miners and aggregates producers
ideas.sector_focus: Materials and energy: coal (met and thermal), silver/gold, rare earths, potash, lime, frac sand, aggregates and cement
ideas.mechanism: Every US mine operator must file MSHA Form 7000-2 within 30 days after each quarter with employee-hours and (for coal) tons produced per mine, and MSHA publishes the quarterly dataset weekly as filings arrive, along with every citation and order. ideas.name: NHTSA Part 573 recall filings and quarterly remedy-completion reports as a warranty-accrual nowcast for RV, powersports, truck, EV and component makers
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer discretionary and industrials: RV and powersports OEMs, trailer and specialty-vehicle makers, EV startups, motorcycle makers, and the component suppliers that self-file equipment recalls
ideas.mechanism: Manufacturers must file a Part 573 defect report with NHTSA within 5 business days of deciding a defect exists, stating the potentially affected unit count (POTAFF) and remedy, and must file quarterly completion reports within 30 days of quarter end with units remedied. A recall decided in the quarter forces a warranty/campaign accrual in that quarter's cost of sales, so the quarter's new campaigns times a per-unit remedy-cost estimate (hardware versus software) nowcasts the accrual, and the completion counts give realized cash cost. For filers in the universe (RV and powersports OEMs, bus and truck makers, EV startups, Lippert-type equipment suppliers), the gap versus consensus gross margin is the edge, because sell-side rarely quantifies campaign accruals before the call.
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter: each campaign is public within ~5 business days of the defect decision, so the quarter's tally is final about a week after quarter end, 20-30 days before earnings. Quarterly completion reports for quarter Q arrive by ~30 days after quarter end (TESTED HERE: 2026-Q3 reports with submission dates through 2026-11-07), i.e., just before or around earnings.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2-3%: about 30 names (REASONED, verify caps): Thor Industries, Winnebago, LCI Industries (Lippert: 11 equipment-recall campaigns filed since 2024, TESTED HERE), Patrick Industries, Polaris, Harley-Davidson, REV Group, Blue Bird, Oshkosh, Wabash, Rivian, Lucid, Fox Factory, Holley, Goodyear, Dorman, Standard Motor Products, Gentherm, Dana, American Axle, Visteon, Modine, Allison Transmission, Garrett Motion, Phinia. Caveat TESTED HERE: the supplier of a defective component is not a structured field (MFR_COMP_NAME is the component's name), and only 4 of 2,849 campaigns since 2024 mention 'supplier' in the text; named-supplier text matches are sparse (Cummins 34, Lear 22, Lippert 14, Bendix 12), so Tier-1 attribution for OEM recalls is weak and the idea works best for companies that file their own recalls.

ideas.name: Proxy-statement (DEF 14A) annual bonus-plan targets versus consensus as a forward guidance-direction signal
ideas.sector_focus: Universe-wide; strongest for mid-caps with a single dominant bonus metric (adjusted EBITDA, revenue, EPS) and wide guidance ranges
ideas.mechanism: The DEF 14A, filed about 90-120 days after fiscal year end, discloses the annual cash-incentive plan's threshold, target and maximum values for the metrics the board chose (adjusted EBITDA, revenue, EPS, free cash flow) plus the prior year's actual achievement and payout percentage. The target is the board-approved internal budget, set with more information than the initial public guidance and usually as a point value rather than a range. A target materially above or below the consensus full-year estimate signals which way guidance and surprises will drift over the next three quarterly announcements; the prior-year payout percentage reveals whether the firm hit plan before the 10-K reconciliations are digested. Applies to any company disclosing numeric targets.
ideas.measurement_window: FY target disclosed in Q1-Q2 proxy season; the signal applies to the following two or three quarterly announcements (30-250 days ahead). Final reading is the proxy filing date (REASONED).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~90% of the universe files DEF 14A; roughly 60-70% disclose numeric annual-plan targets in the CD&A (REASONED, verify on a sample). Examples: any mid-cap industrial or consumer name with an adjusted-EBITDA bonus metric.

ideas.name: JPML monthly pending-action counts per MDL as a litigation-charge nowcast for product-liability defendants
ideas.sector_focus: Healthcare devices, chemicals, consumer products: companies that are primary defendants in a federal multidistrict litigation
ideas.mechanism: The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation publishes a monthly PDF listing every MDL with the number of pending actions. For a company defending a product-liability MDL, the month-over-month change in pending actions drives the litigation accrual, defense-cost run-rate and settlement probability that will show up in the quarter's SG&A, 'other' charges or reserve updates, and sometimes in guidance. Consensus rarely models these numbers, so a surge in new filings during the quarter predicts a charge or elevated legal expense at earnings, or a settlement announcement timed with results. Applies to names such as Solventum (Bair Hugger MDL), Cooper Companies (Paragard MDL), Chemours (AFFF MDL co-defendant), Zimmer Biomet (M/L Taper MDL) and Indivior (Suboxone film MDL) (REASONED list, verify current MDLs).
ideas.measurement_window: Monthly report dated the 1st-15th of each month and published within days (TESTED HERE: November 2, 2026 report posted; archive holds 22 monthly reports from late 2024 to 2026). The last report before earnings covers filings through roughly the end of the quarter, 20-40 days before the release.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1-2%: about 10-20 names at any time that are primary defendants in an active product-liability MDL (REASONED examples above; several large MDL defendants such as 3M, J&J, Bayer are outside the cap or foreign).

ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A month-over-month increase of at least 25% (and at least 200 actions) in pending actions in an MDL where the company is a primary defendant, measured at least 20 days before the earnings release, predicts a litigation-related charge or a legal-expense increase of at least 10% versus the prior quarter and a negative close T-1 to close T+1 abnormal return versus the sector ETF, controlling for returns on prior litigation-news days, consensus revisions, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Federal product-liability suits against one defendant are consolidated into an MDL, and plaintiff firms file in waves driven by advertising and bellwether outcomes. Companies must accrue when a loss becomes probable and estimable and must disclose reasonably possible losses, so filing surges translate into quarterly charges and footnote changes that the JPML count anticipates.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Companies often accrue nothing until a settlement framework exists, adjusted EPS excludes litigation charges, filing surges reflect plaintiff marketing rather than merit, and the stock reaction is concentrated on bellwether verdicts and settlement announcements rather than on earnings day.

ideas.name: openFDA MAUDE device-event report velocity per manufacturer and product code as a recall and quality-cost lead
ideas.sector_focus: Healthcare devices ex-biotech: insulin pumps and CGMs, cardiovascular and neuro devices, orthopedic implants, surgical consumables
ideas.mechanism: Device makers must file medical device reports (MDRs) with FDA within 30 days of learning of a malfunction, injury or death, and openFDA republishes them weekly with manufacturer, product code, event type and date received. A sustained rise in monthly MDR counts for a company's key product code, normalized by installed base or revenue, precedes field actions, Class I/II recalls, elevated warranty and remediation costs and, for consumables, lower utilization or share loss. The edge is that the sell-side reacts to the recall announcement, not to the report velocity that precedes it. Applies to companies with one or two dominant device families.

ideas.name: Mid-quarter non-earnings 8-K items (2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 3.01, 4.01, 4.02, 5.02 finance-officer departures) as a universe-wide negative-surprise flag
ideas.sector_focus: Universe-wide; most informative for small caps with thin analyst coverage
ideas.mechanism: Within four business days of the triggering event, companies must file an 8-K under Item 2.04 (triggering events accelerating obligations), 2.05 (exit or disposal costs), 2.06 (material impairments), 3.01 (delisting notice), 4.01 (auditor change), 4.02 (non-reliance on prior financials) or 5.02 (officer departures, which can be classified as CFO/CAO versus other). These items are structured in the EDGAR submissions API's 'items' field and arrive weeks before the Item 2.02 earnings 8-K. A mid-quarter filing of any of these means the quarter will carry charges, restatement or control risk, or a leadership gap; small-cap consensus revisions lag such filings, so a composite flag predicts negative EPS surprise and a negative earnings-day reaction beyond the filing-day move. Applies to every filer in the universe.
ideas.measurement_window: Window from the prior earnings date to 5 trading days before the next scheduled release; the final reading is the last qualifying 8-K acceptance timestamp. Filings are public within 4 business days of the event (SEC rule), typically 10-70 days before earnings.
ideas.universe_coverage: 100% of the ~1,300 names are covered; the flag fires for roughly 5-10% of firm-quarters (REASONED, to be measured in Phase 1).

ideas.cost: $0 (SEC requires only a declared User-Agent and under 10 requests per second)
ideas.who_already_knows: Quant funds and news-analytics vendors parse 8-K items in-house (REASONED), so the filing-day reaction is efficient. LITERATURE: Lerman and Livnat (2010, Review of Accounting Studies, 'The New Form 8-K Disclosures') document significant filing-day reactions to the expanded 8-K items; whether a residual earnings-day effect remains is UNKNOWN and is the testable question. Priced in: filing-day move yes; subsequent consensus adjustment incomplete for thinly covered names (REASONED).
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: None of the brief's listed alt-data vendors sell 8-K item signals; news-analytics providers (not named, UNKNOWN) may encode them.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free, structured, timestamped and universe-wide; used not as a filing-day trade but as a conditioning flag and control for the other nine signals, with the earnings-day residual as the target.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: Filing of an 8-K containing Item 2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 3.01, 4.01, 4.02 or a 5.02 CFO/CAO departure between the prior earnings date and 5 trading days before the next scheduled release predicts a negative EPS surprise versus final consensus and a negative close T-1 to close T+1 abnormal return versus the sector ETF, controlling for the filing-day return, consensus revisions, size, momentum and sector.
ideas.industry_context: Since 2004 the SEC has required companies to disclose a list of specific corporate events within four business days, long before the quarterly report. Impairments, restructuring charges, restatements and auditor or CFO changes are the events most associated with bad quarters.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Markets price the 8-K at filing and analysts of larger names revise promptly, so the earnings-day residual may be zero or even positive (kitchen-sink quarter followed by relief); the flag is correlated with low momentum and small size, which the controls must absorb; and these filings are rare enough that a 2-10 day event strategy gets few trades per quarter.
ideas.canonical_name: Mid-quarter negative-event 8-K items flag

ideas.name: Quarter-end unit counts and closure / coming-soon flags from store-locator sitemaps and location pages
ideas.sector_focus: Multi-unit chains: fast-casual and casual restaurants, fitness clubs, car wash, wax/personal-care services, specialty retail (company-operated and franchised)
ideas.mechanism: For multi-unit chains reported revenue is units x average unit volume, and the quarter-end system unit count plus net openings are disclosed only at the release. Location pages (Yext/Rio-SEO style locations.<brand>.com or /locations/ paths) are created at or just before opening, often flagged 'coming soon', and are removed or flagged 'permanently closed' at closure. A daily diff of the location sitemap gives net unit adds through the quarter-end day, one day after quarter end, which can be compared with the pro-rated annual opening guide. Opening slippage versus guide implies a revenue shortfall and a unit-growth guidance cut; a spike in removals precedes closure/impairment charges. (REASONED mechanism; TESTED HERE that sitemaps expose per-location pages for Sweetgreen, European Wax Center, Life Time and Wingstop.)
ideas.measurement_window: Full fiscal quarter, daily snapshots; final reading is the quarter-end-day count (available T+1 after quarter end, typically 25-45 days before the release). 'Coming soon' page count is a forward read on next quarter's openings.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~7%: about 90 names. Restaurants (WING, BROS, SG, CAVA, SHAK, TXRH, FWRG, PTLO, KRUS, CAKE, EAT, BLMN, BJRI, JACK, PZZA, DIN, LOCO, WEN, DPZ), fitness/wellness (PLNT, LTH, XPOF, EWCZ), car wash (MCW), specialty retail (FIVE, OLLI, BOOT, ASO, FND, LESL, SFM, GO, ARHS, RH, WRBY). TESTED HERE 2026-11-11 counts: Sweetgreen 299 /locations/ pages; European Wax Center 1,045 center-level pages (depth-3 URLs) on locations.waxcenter.com; Life Time 458 distinct state/club slugs; Wingstop locations sitemap index with 14 sub-sitemaps of ~10,000 URLs each (includes per-location menu pages, needs filtering).

ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side models unit growth from company guidance and press releases and does occasional manual locator checks; Thinknum has marketed store-location/store-count datasets (REASONED). Placer.ai sells foot traffic, not unit rosters. Consensus assumes the guided opening cadence, so the exploitable gap is intra-quarter slippage in opening timing and unannounced closures, which are rarely priced before the release for sub-$5B names (REASONED).
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Thinknum (store locations/counts; REASONED), Placer.ai (traffic only)
ideas.why_ours_differs: Exact quarter-end cut from daily sitemap diffs, free, with per-page creation/removal dates and 'coming soon'/'temporarily closed' flags; vendors deliver monthly aggregates and do not cover sub-$2B chains well.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A shortfall of at least 10% in net new location pages versus the pro-rated annual opening guide over the fiscal quarter, measured 1 day after quarter end (at least 20 days before the release), predicts a negative revenue surprise and a negative T+1/T+2 abnormal return versus the sector ETF, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Unit-growth chains are valued on new-unit cadence, and revenue models are built unit by unit, so opening delays are punished at earnings. Location pages are SEO assets created at opening and deleted at closure, so the public web carries the unit roster in near real time.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Openings are often pre-announced and 'coming soon' pages tip sell-side; page creation can lead or lag the actual opening by weeks; franchised closures may be removed late; AUV dilution from new units can matter more than count; several target sites bot-block the container.

ideas.name: Nationwide in-stock unit counts and model-year mix from OEM-hosted dealer inventory search tools
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer discretionary leisure-vehicle and outdoor-equipment OEMs selling through independent dealers (powersports, RV, marine, standby generators, outdoor power)
ideas.mechanism: These OEMs recognise revenue on wholesale shipment to dealers, so quarterly revenue depends on dealers' willingness to take units, which is governed by dealer floor-plan inventory. Several OEMs host nationwide 'find in-stock inventory' searches listing units by dealer, model and model year. A daily count of listed new units, and the share that are prior-model-year, measures channel inventory: rising stock with a rising stale share precedes shipment cuts, promotional support (margin) and guidance cuts; falling stock precedes restocking shipments. The quarter-end reading is available T+1. (REASONED; OEM commentary on dealer inventory is a standard earnings topic, LITERATURE-free.)
ideas.measurement_window: Daily through the quarter; final reading is quarter-end listed units and prior-model-year share, plus the 4-week trend into quarter end.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2%: about 20-25 names: HOG, PII, WGO, THO, MBUU, MCFT, BC, FOXF (derivative), GNRC, TTC, LCII (derivative), REVG, BLBD; dealer-side listings for CWH (RV), HZO and ONEW (marine) as cross-checks. TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: winnebago.com/dealers 200 and malibuboats.com/dealer-locator 200 (dealer locators only, inventory endpoints not found in static HTML); harley-davidson.com guessed inventory URLs 404 and polaris.com 403 from the container, so exact inventory endpoints are UNKNOWN until discovered in a browser.

ideas.who_already_knows: OEMs discuss dealer inventory qualitatively each quarter (Harley gives dealer inventory units; Polaris gives dealer inventory percentage changes) and sell-side runs quarterly dealer surveys/calls (REASONED). Consensus embeds last quarter's commentary, not the intra-quarter path or model-year mix; the gap is the end-of-quarter level versus what management implied (REASONED).
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: None confirmed for OEM-site inventory counts (UNKNOWN). RV Trader / Boat Trader are listing marketplaces, not data vendors (REASONED).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Daily nationwide count with model-year mix, free, versus quarterly dealer surveys with small samples; cross-checked against dealer-group listings.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A rise of at least 15% quarter-over-quarter in OEM-listed new in-stock units with the prior-model-year share up at least 5 points, measured at quarter end (at least 20 days before the release), predicts negative revenue and gross-margin surprises and negative T+1/T+2 abnormal returns for powersports, RV and marine OEMs, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Leisure-vehicle OEMs sell to dealers that finance inventory on floor plans; when lots fill, OEMs cut shipments and fund promotions, hitting revenue and margin a quarter before retail demand weakness is visible. Model-year changeovers make stale inventory visible in listings.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Listings may be opt-in and cover only part of the dealer base; units in transit or allocated may be counted; management already quantifies dealer inventory on calls; seasonality is strong; OEM site terms may prohibit automated access.

ideas.name: Product-page ship-date and lead-time wording as a backlog gauge for made-to-order durables
ideas.sector_focus: Home furnishings (made-to-order upholstery and case goods), standby generators, EV makers with configurators, premium fitness equipment, build-to-order boats and RVs
ideas.mechanism: Made-to-order and configured goods publish delivery windows ('ships in 8-12 weeks', 'estimated delivery: month') on product pages or configurators because customers must be told when goods arrive. Lengthening quoted lead times mean the order book is growing faster than capacity (revenue recognised later, pricing power up); shortening lead times alongside discounts mean order intake is slowing (next-quarter revenue and guidance risk, under-absorption pressure on margin). A catalogue-weighted lead-time index is read daily and finalised at quarter end, T+1. (REASONED.)
ideas.measurement_window: Daily through the quarter by product family; quarter-end index level and the change over the final 6 weeks of the quarter.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2%: about 20-25 names: RH, ARHS, LOVE, LZB, ETD, SNBR, Somnigroup/TPX, PTON, GNRC, RIVN, LCID, MBUU, MCFT, WGO, THO (Airstream build-to-order). TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: rh.com product URL 200 but a 2 KB client-rendered shell; lovesac.com/sactionals 200 with no ship-in wording in static HTML; rivian.com/configurations/list?model=R1S 200 containing a 'DeliveryTimingModal' copy key (delivery timing rendered client-side); generac.com home-backup page 200 without static lead-time text; arhaus.com 430 (blocked). So headless rendering is required and exact fields are UNKNOWN until rendered.

No systematic daily tracking for furniture names is known to me (UNKNOWN). Management's last backlog comment is priced; the intra-quarter drift is not.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: None confirmed for lead-time text (UNKNOWN); Edited and DataWeave track price and assortment, not quoted lead times (REASONED)
ideas.why_ours_differs: Daily SKU-level text-derived backlog proxy, free; no vendor packages quoted lead times for small-cap durables.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A shortening of at least 2 weeks in the catalogue-weighted quoted lead time over the final 6 weeks of the quarter, measured 1 day after quarter end (at least 20 days before the release), predicts a negative revenue-guidance change and negative T+1/T+2 abnormal returns for made-to-order durables makers, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Made-to-order manufacturers reveal backlog through quoted delivery windows, which is the only public forward indicator for these businesses between quarterly reports. Backlog length also drives pricing power and plant absorption, so it maps to both revenue timing and margin.

ideas.name: Apple App Store userRatingCount velocity and release cadence for transaction-prompted apps of chains, airlines and service companies
ideas.sector_focus: Restaurants, fitness, car wash, airlines and travel, consumer-health/telehealth, specialty retail and marketplaces (not venture-style consumer tech)
ideas.mechanism: Apple's lookup and search API returns cumulative `userRatingCount`, `averageUserRating`, `version` and `currentVersionReleaseDate` for any app. Apps that prompt for a rating after a transaction (order, check-in, wash, flight) accrue ratings roughly in proportion to transacting users, so the seasonally adjusted daily first difference nowcasts transaction and active-member growth through the quarter. A collapse in release cadence signals engineering cuts, and a dip in the rating average signals app outages that depress digital sales. Final reading T+1 after quarter end. (REASONED; TESTED HERE that counters and version dates are exposed.)
ideas.measurement_window: Daily cumulative counts archived; quarter sum of daily increments versus the same quarter a year earlier; days between version releases; final at quarter end.

ideas.name: State-filed Franchise Disclosure Documents: Item 20 outlet turnover and projected openings, Item 19 unit economics for listed franchisors
ideas.sector_focus: Franchisors in restaurants, fitness, personal-care services, automotive services, hotels and tax preparation
ideas.mechanism: Franchisors must update their FDD within 120 days of fiscal year end and file it in registration states; California (DFPI DocQNet), Minnesota (CARDS), Wisconsin (DFI) and Indiana publish the PDFs free. Item 20 tables list outlets opened, closed, terminated, transferred and reacquired by state for three years plus projected openings for the coming year by state; Item 19 gives AUV and margin distributions by cohort. Comparing projected openings with public unit-growth guidance, tracking terminated/ceased-operation counts (franchisee distress) and cohort AUV trends gives a forward read on royalty revenue, unit guidance and franchisee health ahead of the Q1 and Q2 releases. This is regulatory exhaust that lands on digital state portals. (REASONED mechanism; portals TESTED HERE reachable.)
ideas.measurement_window: Annual: prior fiscal-year outlet tables and next-year projected openings, filed late March to April and posted by states within days to weeks; the first affected release is the Q1 report (lead often only 10-30 days), subsequent releases 60-150 days.

ideas.name: Off-cycle fiscal-quarter peers as nowcasters: reporters whose quarter overlaps two of the three months of calendar-quarter peers and lands 3-6 weeks earlier
ideas.sector_focus: Multiple: homebuilding and building products (Lennar/KB Home, Nov FY), freight and logistics (FedEx, May FY), railcars (Greenbrier, Aug FY), industrial distribution (MSC Industrial, Aug FY), coatings and building materials (RPM, May FY), packaged food (General Mills, Conagra, Lamb Weston, May FY; McCormick, Nov FY), restaurants (Darden, May FY), office furniture (Steelcase, Feb FY; MillerKnoll, May FY), steel processing (Commercial Metals, Aug FY; Worthington, May FY), EMS (Jabil, Aug FY), uniforms/services (Cintas, May FY), footwear and apparel (Nike, May FY)
ideas.mechanism: A firm whose fiscal quarter ends one month before the calendar quarter reports results and next-quarter guidance that cover two of the three months its calendar-quarter peers and customers are still accumulating, and it does so 3-6 weeks before they report (e.g., Lennar's Sep-Nov quarter reported mid-December predicts the Oct-Dec quarter that Taylor Morrison, Meritage, M/I Homes and the building-products names report in late January-February; Greenbrier's Sep-Nov quarter reported in early January predicts Trinity and GATX; FedEx's Sep-Nov quarter reported mid-December predicts Forward Air, Hub Group, ArcBest and Saia). The off-cycle reporter's revenue surprise and guidance versus its own consensus is therefore a partial nowcast of the peers' quarter, not just a correlated prior-quarter print. LITERATURE: intra-industry information transfer is well documented (Ramnath 2002, Journal of Accounting Research; Hou 2007, Review of Financial Studies on industry lead-lag), and Thomas and Zhang (2008, Journal of Accounting Research, 'Overreaction to intra-industry information transfers?') report that late announcers' prices overreact to early announcers' news and partially reverse at their own announcement, so the sign must be tested rather than assumed.
ideas.measurement_window: Two of the three months of the target's quarter (the overlap), plus the predictor's guidance for the following quarter, which spans the target's third month. Available 14-35 days before the target's release depending on the pair.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~15-20%: 200-250 names in sub-industries that contain at least one off-cycle reporter. Example targets (REASONED; verify caps): Taylor Morrison (TMHC), Meritage (MTH), M/I Homes (MHO), Installed Building Products (IBP), Trinity (TRN), GATX (GATX), Forward Air (FWRD), Hub Group (HUBG), ArcBest (ARCB), Texas Roadhouse (TXRH), Brinker (EAT), HNI (HNI), Post (POST), TreeHouse (THS), Olympic Steel (ZEUS), Ryerson (RYI), Plexus (PLXS), Benchmark (BHE).

ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side publishes explicit read-through notes after Lennar, FedEx, Nike, Darden, General Mills and MSC prints, and the peers' prices move on the predictor's day, so the first-order transfer is priced (LITERATURE, Thomas and Zhang 2008). The exploitable part is the residual for low-coverage small-caps after controlling for the peer's reaction on the predictor's day, and the possibility that the sign is a reversal rather than a continuation.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: No vendor known to sell a fiscal-offset pair map (UNKNOWN); Bloomberg peer/supply-chain functions provide the raw relationships.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Systematic pair construction from XBRL fiscal-period-end data across the whole universe, with the predictor's guidance quantified against its own consensus, and the target's day-of reaction used as a control to isolate under- or over-reaction.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A revenue or guidance surprise of at least two standard deviations (relative to the predictor's own surprise history) by an off-cycle reporter whose fiscal quarter overlaps at least two months of the target's quarter, measured at least 10 days before the target's release, predicts a same-sign close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus the sector ETF and a same-sign revenue surprise for the not-yet-reported peers, controlling for the peer's abnormal return on the predictor's announcement day, 30-day consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum; a significant opposite-sign coefficient would instead confirm the Thomas-Zhang reversal.
ideas.industry_context: Roughly a fifth of US companies use fiscal years that end in months other than December, so within many sub-industries one firm closes its books a month early and reports while its peers are still inside their quarter. Its print is the only audited look at the same demand months before the peers speak.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: The literature already documents both the transfer and an overreaction-then-reversal, and read-through notes are a sell-side staple, so any residual is small; the predictor's mix (Lennar's geographies, FedEx's parcel mix) differs from the targets; and what looks like a lead may just be post-earnings-announcement drift of the predictor transmitted through factor exposure.

vet.reject_reason: This is the intra-industry information transfer / industry lead-lag effect, published since the 1990s and shown by Chung, Hrazdil and Trottier (2015, 2014) to have decayed to insignificance in recent samples, especially under GICS peer definitions. The first-order transfer is priced on the predictor's day and sell-side read-through notes after Lennar, FedEx, Nike, Darden and General Mills are routine, so the only residual claimed (after controlling for the day-of reaction) is exactly what the overreaction literature measured and later found gone. The free data cannot supply historical revenue consensus for the predictor (Nasdaq forecast is snapshot-only), so the 'surprise vs own consensus' predictor is not backtestable at $0 without proxies. Expected residual is below this account's costs.
vet.red_team: What looks like a lead is the predictor's post-earnings-announcement drift transmitted through sector beta and industry momentum (Hou 2007), plus a mix mismatch (Lennar geographies vs small homebuilders, FedEx parcel vs LTL); after the day-of reaction, 30-day revisions, sector and momentum controls the coefficient is an unstable sign test on roughly 200 names, and the 2015 evidence says the market already corrected this.

ideas.name: REIT supplemental tenant tables as an early store-count and distress feed for retail, restaurant and fitness tenants
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer discretionary and staples: multi-unit brick-and-mortar retailers, restaurants, fitness and consumer services with 100+ leased locations
ideas.mechanism: Shopping-center, mall and net-lease REITs (Kimco, Regency, Brixmor, Phillips Edison, Kite Realty, Tanger, Macerich, Agree Realty, NNN REIT, Essential Properties, Four Corners, NetSTREIT, Acadia, Urban Edge, InvenTrust, Federal Realty) file quarterly supplemental packages as 8-K EX-99 exhibits listing their top tenants with number of leases/stores and ABR, plus tenant watch-lists, bankruptcy exposure tables and lease-termination fee income. REITs report in late October/January/April/July, before January-fiscal-year retailers (late Nov/Feb/May/Aug) and before calendar-quarter restaurants and fitness chains that report in the second half of the following month. Aggregating one tenant's lease count across 15-20 REIT supplementals quarter over quarter gives a sampled net opening/closure count 3-6 weeks before the tenant discloses unit growth, and a tenant's appearance on a watch-list or in a bankruptcy table is a distress read-through. Applies to tenants whose revenue growth is unit-driven and whose consensus embeds a guided opening count.
ideas.measurement_window: The REIT's quarter, which coincides with the calendar quarter; for January-fiscal-year retailers the REIT quarter covers two of the retailer's three months, for calendar-quarter restaurants and fitness chains all three. Available 14-35 days before the tenant's release.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~6%: about 80 names. Likely fits (REASONED; verify caps): Five Below (FIVE), Ollie's (OLLI), Academy Sports (ASO), Boot Barn (BOOT), Floor and Decor (FND), Planet Fitness (PLNT), Dave and Buster's (PLAY), Sally Beauty (SBH), Shake Shack (SHAK), Cava (CAVA), First Watch (FWRG), Life Time (LTH), Mister Car Wash (MCW), Sweetgreen (SG).

ideas.who_already_knows: REIT analysts track tenant exposure from the REIT's side and retail analysts track openings from the retailer's own disclosures and press releases; cross-REIT aggregation per tenant is not a standard product (REASONED). Coresight Research publishes aggregate US store opening/closure tallies (REASONED), and Placer.ai sells foot traffic, which is a different measure. For mid-cap tenants the sampled store-count change is unlikely to be in consensus before the print.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Placer.ai (foot traffic, not unit counts); Coresight Research (store closure tallies, REASONED); Green Street (REIT and tenant analytics, REASONED). None known to sell per-tenant cross-REIT lease-count diffs (UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free regulatory exhaust, tenant-mapped across landlords, measured as net unit change and watch-list mentions, and timed to the 3-6 week gap between landlord and tenant reporting.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A net change of at least 3% quarter over quarter in a tenant's aggregated lease count across at least 10 REIT supplementals, or a first appearance on any landlord's watch-list or bankruptcy table, measured at least 10 days before the tenant's earnings release, predicts a same-sign revenue surprise versus consensus and close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus XLY (negative for watch-list appearances), controlling for guided unit growth, 30-day consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Most US retailers and restaurant chains lease their locations, and a handful of public REITs own tens of thousands of those boxes; because landlords report before tenants and must disclose top-tenant exposure, the landlord's filings are an early, independent sample of the tenant's unit base and credit health.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: REIT portfolios are a small, non-random sample of a tenant's fleet, and lease counts change when the REIT buys or sells centers rather than when the tenant acts; openings are already guided and pre-announced; unit growth moves revenue modestly compared with comparable-store sales; and lease signing precedes store opening by quarters.
ideas.canonical_name: REIT supplemental tenant tables as store-count and distress feed
