vet.reject_reason: Top-tenant tables in REIT supplementals list only the top 20-40 tenants by ABR, which are mostly mega-caps outside the universe (TJX, Ross, Kroger, Dollar Tree, Burlington); a mid-cap tenant appears in a handful of landlords covering perhaps 5-15% of its fleet, so a 3% QoQ change in sampled lease count is dominated by the REIT's own acquisitions, dispositions and redevelopments rather than tenant action. Watch-list and bankruptcy tables appear after the distress is public (dockets, press). Openings are guided and pre-announced, and Coresight, dataplor and Placer already sell openings/closures at scale; the REIT version is neither faster (supplementals land 3-4 weeks after quarter-end) nor more granular. PDF table extraction across 15-20 formats is high effort for a sampled, landlord-driven count.
vet.red_team: The measured quantity is landlord portfolio turnover, not tenant unit growth: a Kimco disposition of three centers removes a tenant's leases with no change in the tenant's fleet, and lease signing precedes opening by quarters, so any correlation with the tenant's revenue surprise is spurious or already in guided unit counts.

ideas.name: Earnings-triggered early lock-up release clauses in 424B4 prospectuses as a forced-supply overhang in the post-earnings window of recent IPOs
ideas.sector_focus: All sectors; companies within roughly 12 months of IPO with market cap above $500M and listed options
ideas.mechanism: Since about 2020 many IPO lock-up agreements release a tranche (often 15-35% of locked shares, sometimes all shares if the stock trades a set percentage above the IPO price) a fixed number of trading days after the company's first or second earnings release following the IPO, instead of at a fixed 180-day date (REASONED; widely reported in 2020-2021 prospectuses such as Snowflake, Airbnb and DoorDash; must be verified per 424B4). The earnings announcement is therefore also a mechanical supply event: employees, VCs and pre-IPO holders can sell from T+1 or T+2, which skews the post-announcement price path negative regardless of the surprise and mutes the reaction to a beat. LITERATURE: fixed-date lock-up expirations carry roughly -1% to -3% abnormal returns with volume spikes (Field and Hanka 2001, Journal of Finance; Bradley, Jordan, Roten and Yi 2001, Journal of Financial Research); the earnings-conditional version concentrates that supply inside the 2-10 day event window this program trades. Applies to any recent IPO whose 424B4 lock-up section references an earnings release.
ideas.target: abnormal return in the post-event window (supply overhang), secondary: EPS/revenue surprise reaction asymmetry
ideas.measurement_window: Binary clause flag plus releasable shares divided by average daily volume, both known from the 424B4 at IPO; the earnings date is confirmed roughly 30 days ahead. Fully available before the event.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2-4%: 25-50 names per year (recent IPOs above $500M with listed options). Types: 2024-2026 software, consumer, industrial and healthcare-services IPOs; candidate names to verify (REASONED): Rubrik (RBRK), Ibotta (IBTA), Loar (LOAR), ServiceTitan (TTAN), Hinge Health (HNGE), StubHub (STUB); financial-sector IPOs are excluded by the universe rules.

ideas.who_already_knows: IPO desks, underwriters and IPO research shops track lock-up calendars; Renaissance Capital publishes IPO calendars and lock-up expirations (REASONED). Fixed-date expiries are crowded; the earnings-conditional clauses are tracked less systematically and are not part of EPS consensus (REASONED). Options implied volatility around these events may already embed the overhang, which is testable from the CBOE snapshots.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Renaissance Capital and IPO Boutique (IPO calendars including lock-up dates, REASONED); Bloomberg carries lock-up expiration fields. None known to flag earnings-conditional release clauses with releasable-shares-to-ADV ratios (UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Reads the clause itself from the prospectus, computes releasable float relative to ADV, and trades the overhang inside the 1-5 day post-earnings window with defined-risk puts or by standing aside on longs.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: For IPOs whose 424B4 ties a lock-up release to an earnings release and whose releasable shares exceed 10 times average daily volume, the close T+1 to close T+5 abnormal return after that earnings release is at least 1.5 percentage points lower than for size- and sector-matched recent IPOs with fixed-date lock-ups, measured with the clause flag set at least 30 days before the event, controlling for the earnings surprise, consensus revisions, sector ETF, size and momentum; and the day-0 reaction to a positive surprise is significantly smaller for the clause group.
ideas.industry_context: IPO lock-ups stop insiders selling for about six months, and underwriters increasingly tie the release to the first post-IPO earnings report so that selling happens when the market has fresh information. That turns a routine earnings date into a scheduled supply shock for thinly floated new listings.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: IPO desks know the clauses, so the overhang may be discounted before the event or embedded in option prices, making puts expensive; many clauses are price-conditional (only if the stock is 25-33% above the IPO price), which creates selection toward winners; and 30-50 events a year give little statistical power after costs.
ideas.canonical_name: Earnings-triggered IPO lock-up release clauses

vet.changes_made: (1) Reclassify: this is an announcement-window supply overhang, not a nowcast of the quarter, so it fails program criterion (a) and must be used as an overlay (stand aside on longs, or a defined-risk put spread only when the CBOE implied move is not elevated vs size-matched recent IPOs), not as an earnings-surprise predictor. (2) Parse the price condition: many clauses release only if the stock trades X% above the IPO price for N of M days; compute the condition state daily and flag an event only when release is unconditional or the condition is met 5 trading days before the print. (3) Correct the examples: per the sources, Snowflake and DoorDash early releases were time-based (91 days) while Airbnb, Reddit, OneStream and Wish were tied to the second earnings release; verify each 424B4's 'Lock-up Agreements' / 'Shares Eligible for Future Sale' section by regex, and distinguish 'blackout pull-forward' clauses (release BEFORE the pre-earnings blackout, i.e. outside the event window) from post-release clauses. (4) Widen the backtest to 2020-2026 IPOs (not the last 12 months) to reach 150+ events; take releasable shares from the prospectus cap table and ADV from Yahoo. (5) Benchmark against fixed-date expirations of matched IPOs to show the earnings-conditional version is distinct from the generic lock-up effect. (6) Watch for underwriter early-release waivers (Kelly, Lv and Twite) announced by 8-K or press release, which move the event date.
vet.revised_hypothesis: Among IPOs within 18 months of listing whose 424B4 ties a lock-up release to an earnings release, where the release is unconditional or its price condition is met 5 trading days before the earnings date, and whose releasable shares exceed 10 times ADV, the close T+1 to close T+5 abnormal return versus the sector ETF is at least 1.5 pp lower than for size-, sector- and age-matched IPOs with fixed-date lock-ups, controlling for the earnings surprise, the pre-event implied move, consensus revisions and momentum; and the T-1 to T+1 reaction to a positive surprise is significantly smaller for the clause group.
vet.revised_universe_coverage: ~2-4%: 25-50 IPO names per year above $500M with listed options, financials excluded; backtest sample 2020-2026 of roughly 150-250 events
vet.red_team: IPO desks, Renaissance IPO Pro and Bloomberg lock-up fields already carry these dates and recent-IPO option IV already embeds the supply, so puts are expensive; the price-conditional variant selects post-IPO winners (momentum / IPO drift confound); and with 25-50 noisy, high-idiosyncratic-vol events a year the measured effect may be the generic fixed-date lock-up expiration return rather than anything earnings-specific.

ideas.name: Used-equipment auction values and dealer used-inventory levels (Sandhills monthly market reports, ELFA, RB Global) as a margin and order nowcast for equipment dealers and OEMs
ideas.sector_focus: Industrials: equipment dealers, truck and trailer OEMs, ag and construction OEMs, equipment rental, truck-lessor fleets
ideas.mechanism: Sandhills Global publishes monthly market reports on used construction equipment, farm machinery, heavy-duty trucks and semi-trailers listed on its marketplaces, with inventory levels and asking and auction values, month over month and year over year (TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: news page live with headlines such as 'Used Truck and Trailer Inventory Down in October as Semi-Trailer Auction Values Jump Nearly 20%' and monthly construction-equipment inventory reports). Used values set trade-in economics: when used values fall while used inventory swells, dealers carry aging used stock and take write-downs (Titan Machinery, Rush Enterprises, Alta Equipment), rental fleets' disposal gains shrink (Herc, Custom Truck), and OEM new orders slow because customers cannot trade up (Wabash, Hyster-Yale, AGCO, CNH, Lindsay, Blue Bird, REV). Rising used values with falling inventory signal replacement demand and pricing power. ELFA's monthly CapEx Finance Index (new equipment-finance volume) corroborates the new-equipment side. Applies to dealers and OEMs whose margins depend on used-equipment values and whose new orders depend on trade-in cycles.
ideas.target: margin (used-inventory write-downs, disposal gains), revenue/orders, guidance
ideas.measurement_window: Months 1-2 of the quarter are certain 10 days before most releases; month 3 arrives 10-20 days after month-end (REASONED from release headlines), so it is available for dealers and OEMs reporting 30+ days after quarter-end and for FY-offset names (Titan Machinery FQ Oct, reports early December).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3%: about 35 names. Likely fits (REASONED; verify caps): Rush Enterprises (RUSHA), Wabash (WNC), AGCO (AGCO), CNH (CNH), Lindsay (LNN), Alamo (ALG), Terex (TEX), Herc (HRI), Custom Truck One Source (CTOS), Allison Transmission (ALSN), Blue Bird (BLBD), REV Group (REVG), Ryder (R), Miller Industries (MLR); Titan Machinery (TITN) and Hyster-Yale (HY) near the $500M floor.

ideas.who_already_knows: Ag and construction sell-side cites Sandhills and auction results, and ACT Research and J.D. Power sell used-truck price data to trucking and OEM analysts (REASONED). The used-value cycle is largely priced for the large OEMs; dealer-level used-inventory write-down risk (Titan, Rush) is covered by few analysts (REASONED).
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Sandhills Global (free headline reports; paid granular data); Rouse Services / RB Global (used-value and rental analytics, REASONED); ACT Research and J.D. Power Valuation Services (used-truck pricing, REASONED).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Uses the free monthly headline indices, maps them to dealer used-inventory exposure (from the dealer's own balance-sheet disclosure of used inventory) rather than to the OEM cycle, and times the read to the dealer's quarter.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A decline of at least 5% YoY in Sandhills auction values combined with a rise of at least 10% YoY in used inventory for a dealer's or OEM's equipment category, measured 10 days before the earnings release, predicts a negative gross-margin surprise and negative close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus XLI, with the effect scaled by used inventory as a share of total inventory, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: New equipment is mostly sold against a trade-in, so the used market sets both the buyer's ability to upgrade and the dealer's inventory risk. Sandhills runs the largest US online marketplaces for used machinery and trucks and publishes monthly inventory and value trends from its own listings.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Category indices are coarse and lag OEM dealer-inventory disclosures that analysts already model; used values are a macro-cyclical factor rather than firm-specific information; report timing varies month to month; and dealer write-downs are often taken at fiscal year-end rather than in the quarter the index moves.
ideas.canonical_name: Sandhills used-equipment values and inventory reports plus ELFA index

Power (paid but syndicated in the trade press the same week) and is cited by sell-side, so it is in consensus; it is macro-cyclical rather than firm-specific, and for truck and trailer OEMs the ACT/FTR order series is the direct nowcast analysts already use. vet.red_team: Used-equipment values are a lagging, macro-cyclical factor largely absorbed by the XLI regression and by the freight/ag cycle variables analysts already model; any residual is a proxy for the industrial cycle, not information about the firm's quarter, and the month-3 reading lands after the print for calendar-quarter OEMs.

ideas.name: Counterparty exhaust: 8-K Item 1.02 terminations and Item 1.01 supply agreements filed by small companies that name a mid-cap customer or supplier
ideas.sector_focus: All sectors; strongest in industrials, healthcare services and devices, technology hardware, consumer brands with concentrated supply chains
ideas.mechanism: When a small public supplier or customer files an 8-K Item 1.02 (termination of a material definitive agreement) or Item 1.01 (entry into one), it must describe the agreement and usually names the counterparty, which is often a larger company for which the change is immaterial or will only be disclosed at earnings. A supplier's termination reveals a customer's program cancellation, insourcing, destocking or capex cut that hits the customer's next quarter (revenue, margin or guidance); a small supplier's new supply agreement reveals a mid-cap customer's capacity expansion or product ramp before the customer guides to it. The SEC submissions API exposes an items field for every 8-K (TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: Kimco rows show '1.01,2.03,3.02,9.01'), and the daily form index lists every 8-K (TESTED HERE: 594 8-Ks on 2025-11-05) whose full-submission header carries 'ITEM INFORMATION' lines (TESTED HERE), so Item 1.01/1.02 filings can be isolated without full-text search; counterparties are tagged by matching the filing text against the universe name list and GLEIF legal names. Applies to any universe company that appears as a named counterparty.
ideas.measurement_window: Event-driven: filings land 4 business days after the triggering event, typically 20-60 days before the counterparty's next earnings release; the signal is the count and classification of counterparty-naming 1.01/1.02 filings in the 90 days before the release.
ideas.universe_coverage: Potentially the whole universe but sparse: perhaps 10-30 universe companies per quarter are named as counterparties (REASONED, ~2% per quarter). Types: mid-cap OEMs named by component suppliers, device makers named by contract manufacturers, retailers named by brand suppliers, pharma-services names named by small drug developers.

ideas.who_already_knows: Users of EDGAR full-text search and Bloomberg filing alerts see the filer's 8-K, and the filer's own stock reprices immediately; the named counterparty's analysts often do not read small filers' 8-Ks (REASONED), consistent with the customer-supplier inattention documented by Cohen and Frazzini (2008, Journal of Finance, 'Economic Links and Predictable Returns') (LITERATURE). Little of it is in the counterparty's consensus before the print.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Quiver Quantitative and similar sell SEC-filing-derived alert data in general (REASONED); no vendor known to sell counterparty-side mapping of Item 1.01/1.02 filings at scale (UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Reads the filing from the counterparty's side, classifies agreement type (supply/customer versus debt/lease/employment, which dominate Item 1.02 counts), and times the signal to the counterparty's earnings rather than to the filer's.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: An 8-K Item 1.02 filed by another company that names a universe member as the counterparty to a supply or customer agreement, filed at least 5 trading days before that member's earnings release, predicts a negative revenue or guidance surprise and negative close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus the sector ETF for the named member, while a counterparty-naming Item 1.01 supply agreement predicts positive capex or revenue guidance, controlling for the member's abnormal return on the filing day, consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: The 8-K rules force a company to disclose within four business days when it enters or terminates a contract material to it, and materiality is judged from the filer's size, so a $300M supplier must disclose a contract that a $10B customer can ignore. The small filer's disclosure is therefore the customer's information, published early.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Events are rare and most Item 1.02 filings concern credit facilities or leases, so classification errors dominate; the terminating party is often the larger counterparty acting in its own interest, which can be positive for it; the impact on a mid-cap's quarter is usually immaterial; and sophisticated holders of the counterparty may already screen for its name in all filings.

vet.reject_reason: Materiality runs the wrong way: an Item 1.02 is filed because the agreement is material to the small filer, and every example found (Methode/Delphi, Amincor/Aldi, XPEL/entrotech, Wright/Novartis) names a counterparty that is either outside the universe or for whom the contract is a rounding error; anything large enough to move a mid-cap's quarter would be disclosed by the mid-cap itself. Cohen-Frazzini's inattention effect runs from a large customer's return to its small suppliers, not from a small filer's 8-K to its large counterparty. Events are roughly 10-30 per quarter across the universe, dominated by credit, lease and employment 1.02s, and the sign is ambiguous when the larger party terminates in its own interest. Data is free and lawful but the signal is too sparse and too immaterial to justify a standalone build; keep the 8-K items filter only as a shared EDGAR utility.
vet.red_team: Materiality asymmetry makes the information set immaterial by construction, so any backtest hit rate would be driven by misclassified credit-facility terminations, sign ambiguity and a handful of lucky events; the named counterparty's analysts do not need to read these filings because the content cannot move its guidance.

ideas.name: Buyback-intensity blackout exposure from 10-Q monthly repurchase tables: the return of a price-insensitive bid after earnings
ideas.sector_focus: All sectors; strongest in mid-cap industrials, consumer and technology names with large repurchase programs relative to trading volume
ideas.mechanism: Companies that buy back stock in the open market suspend discretionary purchases during the quarterly blackout, usually from about two weeks before quarter-end until one or two trading days after the earnings release, unless they buy through a Rule 10b5-1 plan. Part II Item 2 of each 10-Q and 10-K discloses shares repurchased by month, so for each firm one can measure the repurchase run-rate as a share of average daily volume and whether month-3 purchases collapse relative to months 1-2, which identifies discretionary (non-10b5-1) programs. For firms where buybacks exceed 5-10% of ADV, the pre-earnings window lacks a large steady buyer and the post-earnings window (T+2 to T+5) sees it return, which should support the stock after the print and dampen the downside after a miss. LITERATURE: Hong, Wang and Warner (2008, Journal of Financial Economics, 'Firms as buyers of last resort') show repurchasing firms' prices are less sensitive to negative shocks. Applies to firms with active discretionary programs and float-relative intensity high enough to matter.
ideas.target: abnormal return in the post-event window (flow-driven); secondary: EPS surprise via lower share count (minor)
ideas.measurement_window: Trailing two quarters of monthly repurchases from the most recent 10-Q/10-K, available about 40-45 days after the prior quarter-end, hence roughly 45 days before the next earnings release; the month-3-collapse flag classifies discretionary programs.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~25-30% have active programs (about 350 names); high-intensity discretionary programs (at least 5% of ADV) perhaps ~8%, about 100 names (REASONED). Types: cash-rich mid-cap industrials, specialty retailers, software and semiconductor names with authorizations above 5% of market cap.

ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side and bank buyback desks publish index-level blackout calendars and the share of S&P 500 market cap in blackout (REASONED), so the aggregate effect is widely discussed; firm-level intensity relative to ADV combined with a discretionary-versus-10b5-1 classification from the monthly table is not standard (REASONED). The flow is not in consensus EPS at all; the question is whether the post-print drift is already arbitraged.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: No vendor known to sell firm-level monthly repurchase intensity with blackout classification (UNKNOWN); Bloomberg and S&P carry quarterly buyback totals.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Firm-level, monthly, free from the 10-Q table, scaled by ADV, and classified by whether purchases stop in month 3, which is the actual marker of the mechanism.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: For firms whose trailing two-quarter open-market repurchases exceed 5% of average daily volume and whose month-3 purchases are below 30% of the months 1-2 average, measured at least 40 days before the earnings release, the close T+1 to close T+5 abnormal return versus the sector ETF is at least 0.8 percentage points higher than for size-, sector- and surprise-matched non-repurchasers, controlling for the earnings surprise, consensus revisions, size, momentum and the value factor.
ideas.industry_context: Corporate buybacks are one of the largest sources of equity demand, but insider-trading rules push most companies to stop buying in the weeks before results unless they pre-committed through a 10b5-1 plan. The pause and resumption are visible after the fact in the monthly repurchase table every 10-Q must include.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Many firms now run 10b5-1 plans straight through the blackout, so the flow never stops; the effect is likely a few tenths of a percent, below this account's trading costs; buyback intensity proxies for value and quality factors; and firms pause programs precisely when results are weak, confounding the sign.

vet.reject_reason: The one practitioner test found (HedgeFundAlpha) reports no significant return difference around blackouts even for heavy-buyback firms, and the academic literature documents the timing pattern but not a tradeable return effect. The plausible firm-level effect is a few tenths of a percent over T+1 to T+5, below this account's round-trip costs, and the flow (5-10% of ADV) is small relative to post-earnings volume, which runs 3-10x normal. The monthly table is untagged HTML, so building ~350 firms x 8 quarters of parsing is high effort. The month-3-collapse flag is confounded: firms pause when results are weak and 10b5-1 plans run through blackouts. Hong, Wang and Yu (not 'Warner') concerns return variance of unconstrained firms, not announcement drift. The mechanism never produces an EPS or revenue surprise, so it fails program criterion (a).
vet.red_team: Buyback intensity is a value, quality and low-volatility factor proxy; the 'support' after the print is indistinguishable from the known lower downside variance of cash-rich firms, and the measured drift would be the factor loading, not the flow.

ideas.name: Securitization-trust 10-D monthly servicer reports as a nowcast of captive-finance credit losses (Harley-Davidson, CarMax)
ideas.sector_focus: Consumer companies with SEC-registered captive-finance ABS: motorcycles (Harley-Davidson Financial Services) and used-auto retail (CarMax Auto Finance)
ideas.mechanism: Public auto/motorcycle ABS trusts must file a Form 10-D each month with the servicer report: pool balance, 30/60/90+ day delinquencies, net losses and recoveries. HDFS contributes a large share of Harley's operating income and CarMax Auto Finance income (net of its loan-loss provision) is a key swing in CarMax EPS, so pool-balance-weighted delinquency and loss trends across the active trusts give the direction of the provision 2-8 weeks before the parent reports. Applies to consumer discretionary names whose captive lender issues publicly registered ABS (Lithia's LAD trusts appear to be 144A-only: no 10-D found, TESTED HERE).
ideas.measurement_window: Monthly collateral performance. TESTED HERE: Harley-Davidson Motorcycle Trust 2024-B 10-Ds filed 2026-10-28 (Sept), 2026-09-29 (Aug), 2026-08-27 (Jul), i.e. ~27 days after month-end, so for a calendar quarter months 1-2 are in hand ~3-5 weeks before Harley's report and month 3 arrives about the same day. CarMax Auto Owner Trust 10-Ds filed ~15th of the following month (TESTED HERE on trust 2018-2 history), so all three months of CarMax's Feb/May/Aug/Nov quarters are filed ~10 days before its earnings.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.2%: 2 names today, Harley-Davidson (HOG) and CarMax (KMX), each with a finance segment material to EPS; extend if other universe names register public ABS (check quarterly via EDGAR company search for 'Owner Trust'/'Receivables Trust' with the parent's name).

REASONED: the credit trend is semi-public but rarely mapped to the parent's EPS surprise; management typically guides provision direction on the prior call, so part of the trend is in consensus.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Intex and Bloomberg distribute structured-finance collateral performance to fixed-income desks at institutional prices; no vendor known to sell this as an equity-earnings signal for HOG/KMX (UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free from EDGAR, aggregated across all live trusts and aligned to the parent's fiscal quarter and earnings date, with an explicit mapping to the finance-segment provision line that equity consensus models.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A rise of at least 25 bp YoY in the pool-balance-weighted 60+ day delinquency rate across the issuer's active public trusts for the quarter's filed months, measured 7 days before the earnings release, predicts a negative EPS surprise (finance-segment provision above consensus) and negative T-1 to T+1 abnormal return versus XLY, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Harley's and CarMax's captive lenders fund themselves partly through public securitizations, and Reg AB forces monthly disclosure of how those loans are performing. Those same loans are a representative slice of the receivables whose loss provision runs through the parent's income statement.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Securitized pools are a selected, seasoning-biased subset (recent vintages, specific credit tiers) so pool trends can diverge from the on-balance-sheet book; management pre-signals credit trends; and for Harley the equity reacts to motorcycle retail sales far more than to HDFS credit, so the finance line may be a second-order driver of the announcement return.

ideas.name: State liquor-license and food-service-license exhaust (Texas TABC, Florida DBPR) for restaurant and retail unit openings and closures
ideas.sector_focus: Unit-growth restaurant chains, casual dining with closure risk, grocery/c-store chains that hold beer-wine licenses, in Texas and Florida
ideas.mechanism: A new restaurant or alcohol-selling store must obtain a TABC license (Texas) or a DBPR food-service license (Florida) before opening; Texas publishes pending original license applications daily with owner entity, address and submission date, and Florida publishes new food-service licenses by fiscal year plus weekly closure orders. Pending applications therefore reveal the opening pipeline 1-3 months ahead, and license status changes (cancelled/expired/change of ownership) reveal closures and refranchising that companies only disclose at quarter-end. Net licensed units in TX+FL, pro-rated by the chain's share of units in those states, nowcasts unit growth against annual guidance and flags closure clusters.
ideas.measurement_window: Daily status changes; quarter's net openings/closures countable within days of quarter-end (TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: TABC License Information 128,684 rows with status_change_date and original_issue_date; Pending New Primary and Subordinate License Applications dataset returns application_id, owner, address, submission_date, status; Florida newfood_2526.xlsx and EOS weekly closure extract downloaded, extract columns include License Number, Business Name, Address, Date, Conditions for Closure). Pending applications give a forward look of ~30-90 days on openings (REASONED).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3-4%: about 40 names. Restaurants with company-operated TX/FL units: Dutch Bros (BROS), Cava (CAVA), Sweetgreen (SG), Shake Shack (SHAK), First Watch (FWRG), Kura Sushi (KRUS), Portillo's (PTLO), Texas Roadhouse (TXRH), Cheesecake Factory (CAKE), BJ's (BJRI), Bloomin' (BLMN), Dave & Buster's (PLAY), Brinker (EAT), Darden (DRI); retail with beer/wine licenses: Sprouts (SFM), Murphy USA (MUSA), Grocery Outlet (GO), Casey's (CASY, if present in TX/FL). Franchised systems (Wingstop, Dine Brands, Jack in the Box) need franchisee-entity matching and are noisier.

REASONED: partially priced for openings, lightly priced for closures and refranchising.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Placer.ai (foot traffic, includes new-location detection) and SafeGraph (POI open/close datasets) sell at scale; UNKNOWN whether any vendor packages state license pipelines for funds.
ideas.why_ours_differs: License pipelines are leading (filed before opening) rather than lagging POI detection, are free and daily, and carry the legal owner entity, which exposes refranchising and franchisee churn that POI datasets miss.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A shortfall of at least 10% in net new licensed TX+FL units versus the pace implied by the chain's annual unit-growth guidance pro-rated by its TX+FL unit share, measured 3 days before the earnings release, predicts a revenue miss or guidance cut and a negative T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus XLY, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: For growth restaurant chains the stock is a multiple on unit growth, and a slip of a few openings from one quarter to the next changes revenue and the credibility of the annual target. Closures and refranchising are the quiet side of the ledger that management reports only at quarter-end.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Two states are a partial sample; license issue dates can precede openings by months or follow soft openings; franchise entities obscure the parent; and the most-watched growth chains already drip-feed opening counts, so the residual surprise is small relative to trading costs.

ideas.name: Sentinel-2 finished-goods yard fill at RV plants and dealer lots (white-roof brightness) as a wholesale-shipment and destocking nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: RV manufacturers and their component suppliers; RV dealers
ideas.mechanism: Finished RVs wait outdoors on plant lots in Elkhart County, Indiana and Forest City, Iowa and on dealer lots; their white or light roofs are strongly reflective against asphalt and grass, so the bright-pixel fraction inside a hand-digitized yard polygon in 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery tracks yard occupancy every ~5 days when clear. Rising plant-yard fill means production is outrunning dealer pickup (wholesale shipments slowing, production cuts ahead) which hits Thor and Winnebago revenue and, one week later, LCI and Patrick content sales; falling dealer-lot fill with stable retail means restock orders. Applies to THO (Jayco Middlebury, Keystone Goshen, Heartland, Airstream Jackson Center OH), WGO (Forest City IA, Grand Design Middlebury IN), suppliers LCII and PATK, and dealer Camping World (CWH).
ideas.measurement_window: Whole fiscal quarter at ~5-day revisit; final reading is the last clear scene before the announcement (typically 3-10 days prior; Midwest winter cloud cover will leave gaps, REASONED). Validation step required: confirm that 10 m pixels resolve yard-fill changes at lots holding hundreds of units (REASONED, not yet tested).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.4%: 5 names, Thor (THO), Winnebago (WGO), LCI Industries (LCII), Patrick Industries (PATK), Camping World (CWH); Forest River (Berkshire, private) yards add an industry read.

data_sources.name: Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC item search (sentinel-2-l2a) for scene discovery and COG reads with SAS token
Sentinel Hub Statistical API (CDSE edition) for polygon time-series without downloading scenes
AWS Open Data Sentinel-2 COGs (alternative keyless source)

ideas.cost: $0 (free CDSE account for Statistical API; compute only)
ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side uses RVIA monthly wholesale shipments (published ~3-4 weeks after month-end, so the quarter's last month usually lands after Thor/Winnebago report), dealer surveys and Statistical Surveys retail registrations; management gives dealer-inventory counts quarterly. REASONED: industry-level direction is priced; plant-specific yard inventory is not observed by consensus.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Orbital Insight and RS Metrics sell satellite parking-lot and yard analytics at scale (RS Metrics also covers metals yards); UNKNOWN whether either sells RV plant-yard fill specifically.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Plant-side finished-goods inventory rather than consumer parking traffic, measured on free 10 m imagery at every revisit, for the exact facilities of two tickers plus the suppliers that lag them by a week.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A rise of at least 15% in the yard-fill bright-pixel fraction at Thor and Winnebago plant lots over the fiscal quarter versus the same quarter a year earlier, measured from the last clear Sentinel-2 scene at least 3 days before the announcement, predicts a negative revenue or guidance surprise for THO/WGO and for LCII/PATK the following week, controlling for already-published RVIA wholesale shipments, consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: RV makers build to dealer orders and recognize revenue on wholesale shipment, so dealer destocking shows up first as units piling up on plant lots. Elkhart County assembles most US RVs, concentrating the physical signal in a few square miles.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: 10 m pixels may not resolve occupancy changes reliably, snow and wet pavement change brightness, yards also hold chassis and trailers that are not finished goods, and RVIA data plus dealer checks already give the sell-side the wholesale trend, leaving only timing as the edge.
ideas.seed_item_extended: [physical] Satellite parking-lot car counts (use only as a crowded benchmark; assume mostly priced in)
ideas.canonical_name: Sentinel-2 RV plant and dealer yard fill

vet.reject_reason: Sign of the signal is ambiguous (plant-yard fill rises with transport/driver bottlenecks or chassis staging as readily as with weak dealer pull; RV OEMs largely build against dealer orders, REASONED), two of the four fiscal quarter-ends for THO (Jan 31) and WGO (late Nov, late Feb) fall in the northern-Indiana snow season where white-roof brightness is unreadable, 10 m mixed pixels over gravel/asphalt are an untested instrument, and the quantity consensus actually uses (RVIA monthly wholesale shipments) is public ~3-4 weeks after month-end, which for Thor (reports ~7-8 weeks after quarter end, REASONED) is before the print. No vendor or paper on RV-yard imagery was found; coverage is 5 names. Not worth the hand-digitizing and validation effort at 10% confidence.

ideas.name: Theme-park posted ride wait times (queue-times.com public API) as an in-park attendance and operations index for Six Flags and United Parks
ideas.sector_focus: Regional theme parks and marine parks
ideas.mechanism: Parks post ride wait times continuously; queue-times.com republishes them through a free JSON API with ride open/closed flags. For a given ride capacity, posted waits scale with guests in the park, so the operating-hours average wait across a company's rides, aggregated over the fiscal quarter, is an attendance index, while the share of operating hours with rides flagged closed measures operational problems (staffing, weather, breakdowns) that depress per-capita spend. Applies to Six Flags Entertainment (post-merger company incl. Cedar Fair parks) and United Parks & Resorts (SeaWorld/Busch Gardens), whose quarterly attendance is the headline number.
ideas.measurement_window: Whole fiscal quarter (season-weighted: Q2 Apr-Jun, Q3 Jul-Sep is the critical quarter, Q4 Halloween events); the API is live-only so a 5-10 minute archiver must run continuously (TESTED HERE 2026-11-11: parks.json and /parks/50/queue_times.json return 200 with per-ride wait_time, is_open, last_updated; coverage lists Six Flags Entertainment Corporation 26 parks, Cedar Fair 11, SeaWorld Parks 10). Monthly crowd-calendar HTML pages exist per park (TESTED HERE 200) but their historical depth is UNKNOWN.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.2%: 2 names, Six Flags Entertainment (FUN) and United Parks & Resorts (PRKS); Herschend and Universal parks in the feed are private or part of too-large parents.

data_sources.history_depth: Live only via API; crowd-calendar pages per park and month at https://queue-times.com/parks/50/calendar/2025/07 (depth UNKNOWN)

ideas.cost: $0 (small always-on archiver; confirm commercial-use terms on the queue-times API page: UNKNOWN)
ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side leisure analysts use Placer.ai foot traffic and company mid-quarter commentary; Six Flags and United Parks sometimes pre-announce attendance trends. REASONED: direction of attendance is largely in consensus; ride-downtime and weekend/event-night intensity are not.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Placer.ai sells theme-park foot traffic at scale; Thrill Data and queue-times publish wait statistics publicly; no vendor known to sell wait-time-derived attendance to funds (UNKNOWN).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free, minute-level, measures load inside the park (and ride downtime, a per-cap and cost driver) rather than device visits at the gate, and isolates Halloween-event nights and weather days that drive quarterly surprises.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A decline of at least 5% YoY in operating-hours average posted wait across a company's US parks over the fiscal quarter (ride-capacity-normalized), measured 3 days after quarter-end, predicts attendance below consensus and a negative T-1 to T+1 abnormal return versus XLY, controlling for rain days, consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Regional park operators report attendance and per-capita spend each quarter, and the Q3 summer season decides the year. Attendance is the figure the stocks trade on, and ride availability drives both guest satisfaction and in-park spend.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Posted waits are supply-driven as much as demand-driven (staffing, paid skip-the-line products, virtual queues, new rides), parks with fewer rides open show longer waits at lower attendance, and Placer.ai already gives consensus an attendance read, so only the operations component may be new.
ideas.canonical_name: Theme-park ride wait times as attendance index

vet.reject_reason: Posted wait times are a supply-confounded proxy (rides open, staffing, virtual queues, paid skip-the-line) for attendance, a quantity Placer.ai and INRIX already sell at scale and the companies themselves pre-announce; Thrill Data already publishes daily/weekly wait statistics by park, so the wait-time read is not scarce. The API is live-only (archiver needed, no backtest), the multi-year crowd calendars are JS-rendered pages outside the API's stated terms (.json variants return 406), and coverage is 2 names with one quarter (Q3) that matters, leaving almost no tradeable events. The ride-downtime component is novel but its link to a quarterly per-cap/EBITDA surprise is tenuous.

ideas.name: eBay Browse API new-with-tags listing supply and ask-to-MSRP ratios by brand as a channel-excess and markdown nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Wholesale-heavy apparel, footwear, accessories and outdoor/drinkware brands
ideas.mechanism: When a brand over-ships wholesale or retailers cancel orders, excess current-season goods leak to liquidators and small resellers who list them on eBay as new with tags; the official eBay Browse API returns active-listing counts and asking prices by keyword and condition. A rise in a brand's NWT listing count (normalized by total apparel listings) and a fall in the median ask relative to MSRP for current-season items signals channel inventory excess, which precedes markdowns, wholesale order cuts, gross-margin pressure and guidance cuts. Applies to brands that sell mostly through wholesale partners and off-price rather than their own stores.
ideas.measurement_window: Daily snapshots over the whole fiscal quarter with extra weight on the last 8 weeks; final reading the day before earnings. REASONED: one quarter of history must be built before the first live use because the API is snapshot-only.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~3%: about 35-40 names, e.g. Under Armour (UAA), VF Corp (VFC), Columbia (COLM), Crocs (CROX), Deckers (DECK), Steve Madden (SHOO), Wolverine (WWW), Carter's (CRI), Hanesbrands (HBI), PVH, Capri (CPRI), Tapestry (TPR), G-III (GIII), Oxford (OXM), Levi's (LEVI), YETI, Guess (GES).

ideas.who_already_knows: Brands monitor their own gray-market leakage; sell-side relies on quarterly inventory disclosures and off-price channel checks. REASONED: not systematically used by equity investors; inventory levels are disclosed quarterly so the level is priced, the intra-quarter change is not.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: EDITED and DataWeave sell retail pricing and markdown analytics at scale to retailers; StockX publishes sneaker resale data; UNKNOWN whether any vendor sells eBay NWT supply by brand as a fund signal.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Measures the overflow channel (liquidation supply) rather than first-party shelf prices, uses an official free API with brand-level SKU matching, and is aligned to each brand's fiscal quarter.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A rise of at least 30% YoY in normalized active NWT listing count for a brand's current-season items over the last 8 weeks of its fiscal quarter, measured 2 days before earnings, predicts gross margin below consensus and a negative T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus XLY, controlling for consensus revisions, reported inventory-to-sales ratio, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Apparel and footwear brands recognize wholesale revenue on shipment, so excess stock in the channel surfaces later as markdowns, returns and order cuts. Liquidators and resellers are the pressure valve, and eBay is the largest open marketplace where that valve is observable.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Listing supply also rises with brand popularity and arbitrage demand, counterfeits distort counts, most excess goes to TJX/Ross rather than eBay, and brands already disclose inventory and markdown expectations, so the residual may be noise after costs.
ideas.canonical_name: eBay NWT listing supply and ask-to-MSRP by brand

The data is snapshot-only, so the first YoY reading is 12+ months away and no backtest is possible; the mechanism is weak because most wholesale overflow clears through TJX/ROST/BURL and brand outlets rather than eBay, and NWT listing supply rises with brand heat and reseller arbitrage as much as with channel excess. A first-party alternative (markdown share on brand DTC sites via Shopify products.json, DATA in the Phase 0 file) measures a different mechanism and belongs to a separate candidate (N48-type), not a rescue of this one.

ideas.name: Retailer promotional-email cadence and depth index (self-subscribed mailbox) as a markdown-pressure nowcast for specialty retail and DTC brands
ideas.sector_focus: Specialty apparel, footwear, home furnishings, beauty, sporting goods and DTC brands with large email programs
ideas.mechanism: Retailers reach for deeper and more frequent promotions (site-wide percentage-off, extra-off clearance, lowered free-shipping thresholds, 'last chance' language) when sell-through lags plan, and these messages are sent to every subscriber. Subscribing a dedicated mailbox to ~150 retailers' lists and parsing daily emails yields a promo-intensity index per ticker (frequency x depth x breadth) that, compared with the same weeks a year earlier, reads merchandise-margin pressure for the quarter and end-of-quarter clearance pushes. Applies to retailers with mostly first-party, non-personalized broadcast email programs.
ideas.measurement_window: Daily over the whole fiscal quarter, final reading the day before earnings; backfill history from a public email archive (Milled, UNPROBED, ToS to check) to avoid a one-year warm-up.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~8%: about 100 names, e.g. Abercrombie (ANF), American Eagle (AEO), Urban Outfitters (URBN), Gap (GPS), Levi's (LEVI), Under Armour (UAA), Columbia (COLM), YETI, Crocs (CROX), Figs (FIGS), Revolve (RVLV), RH, Williams-Sonoma (WSM), Wayfair (W), Arhaus (ARHS), La-Z-Boy (LZB), Boot Barn (BOOT), Academy (ASO), Dick's (DKS), Ulta (ULTA), e.l.f. (ELF), Warby Parker (WRBY), Peloton (PTON), Sonos (SONO), Victoria's Secret (VSCO), Bath & Body Works (BBWI), Five Below (FIVE), Petco (WOOF), Chewy (CHWY), Sally Beauty (SBH), Kohl's (KSS), Macy's (M), Dillard's (DDS).

data_sources.name: Own mailbox subscribed to retailer lists (IMAP; any free mail provider); parsed with a rules-based extractor for %-off, breadth, thresholds
Milled (public archive of brand marketing emails, dated by brand) for backfill; ToS and scrape-ability UNKNOWN

ideas.cost: $0 (one mailbox; optional Gmail API key is free)
ideas.who_already_knows: Sell-side does weekly in-store and online promo checks for the biggest names; marketers buy email-intelligence from MailCharts; retailers' guidance embeds the planned promotional calendar. REASONED: broad promo direction is priced; intra-quarter escalation versus plan, especially in the last two weeks, is less so.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: MailCharts sells e-commerce email marketing intelligence; EDITED and DataWeave sell markdown and pricing analytics at scale to retailers; sell-side promo checks are informal. These are not typically consumed as quarter-aligned signals by small funds.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Zero cost, daily, built from the retailer's own broadcast messaging (what it chose to say to all customers), aligned to fiscal quarters and scored for escalation versus the prior year rather than absolute discount level.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: An increase of at least 10 index points in the promo-intensity index (share of days with site-wide >=30% off, weighted by depth and breadth) over the fiscal quarter versus the same quarter a year earlier, measured 1 day before earnings, predicts gross margin and EPS below consensus and a negative T-1 to T+1 abnormal return versus XRT, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Specialty retail profits hinge on merchandise margin, which is set by how much a retailer must mark down to clear inventory. Email is the cheapest lever a merchant pulls when traffic or conversion lags, so promotional cadence reveals the merchant's own read on the quarter.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Promotions follow planned marketing calendars and are increasingly personalized (one mailbox sees one treatment), heavy promotion can accompany strong demand, and for the largest names the sell-side already tracks promo depth weekly, so the residual edge may be confined to mid-cap names with thin coverage.
ideas.canonical_name: Retailer promotional-email intensity index

vet.changes_made: (1) Drop the Milled backfill: milled.com and /terms return 403 from the container, the full-archive is a paid Pro product, and robots.txt disallows /search, /sites/ and category message lists with Content-Signal ai-train=no; mailbox-only, so legal_risk stays 2. (2) Because there is no lawful history, replace the YoY index for the first four quarters with a cross-sectional within-quarter escalation score: promo intensity in the last 14 days of each retailer's fiscal quarter divided by its weeks 1-10 average, ranked across retailers each quarter; switch to YoY once a year of own history exists. (3) Restrict live use to mid-caps with thin sell-side promo coverage and treat the large names (M, KSS, GPS, DKS, ULTA, BBWI) as a control group, since weekly promo checks already exist there. (4) Run two mailboxes per retailer with different personas and no purchase history to detect personalization; drop retailers where the two diverge. (5) Claim a margin-direction effect only (no revenue claim). (6) crowdedness lowered to 2 because MailCharts sells 'promotion rate vs last year' per brand and practitioners (Hedgeye) already count promo emails; signal_noise lowered to 2 for personalization and planned calendars.
vet.revised_hypothesis: Among mid-cap specialty retailers and DTC brands with thin sell-side promo coverage, the top quintile of within-quarter promo escalation (last-14-day promo intensity relative to the quarter's weeks 1-10, measured 1 day before earnings from a self-subscribed mailbox) shows gross margin below consensus and a negative T-1 to T+1 abnormal return versus XRT relative to the bottom quintile, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum; YoY index version to be tested once four quarters of history exist.
vet.revised_universe_coverage: ~5%: roughly 60 mid-cap names after excluding large caps with weekly sell-side promo checks (used as controls); ~100 names collected.

ideas.name: State DOT bid-letting results: apparent-low-bid totals and bid-to-engineer's-estimate ratio per contractor
ideas.sector_focus: Engineering & construction: heavy-civil/highway contractors (Construction Partners, Granite, Sterling Infrastructure, Primoris, Tutor Perini) and USACE dredging (Great Lakes Dredge & Dock).
ideas.mechanism: State DOTs let highway contracts on fixed monthly dates and publish bid tabulations within days: apparent low bidder, bid amount, engineer's estimate and all competing bids. Summing a contractor's apparent-low bids over the quarter nowcasts its new awards and backlog, the number these stocks trade on, and the ratio of winning bid to engineer's estimate plus the gap to the second bidder ('money left on the table') is a leading indicator of future gross margin because contracts are fixed-price and underbidding to fill capacity shows up 2-6 quarters later as margin compression (REASONED). Construction Partners discloses its states (AL, FL, GA, NC, SC, TN, TX), Granite is California/West, Sterling is Texas/Southeast, so each ticker maps to a handful of DOT letting pages; GLDD's revenue is dominated by USACE dredging awards.
ideas.measurement_window: All lettings with bid-opening dates inside the fiscal quarter; last letting results are posted within ~1-10 days of opening, so the final reading is in hand ~Q-end+10 while earnings come 4-6 weeks after Q-end. Awards generally follow bid opening by 30-60 days, so for backlog use award dates (REASONED).
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1%: roughly 8-12 names: ROAD (~$5B), GVA (~$4B), STRL (~$8B), PRIM (~$5B), TPC (~$2B), GLDD (~$0.7B), Orion (ORN, may fall below the size floor), MasTec (MTZ, limited DOT share); caps REASONED.

ideas.name: Rooftop-weighted hail-swath index from NOAA SPC reports and NEXRAD hail signatures as a storm-demand nowcast for roofing and exterior building products
ideas.sector_focus: Building products: asphalt shingles and roofing (Owens Corning, Carlisle), roofing distribution (QXO/Beacon), siding, gutters and exterior (Louisiana-Pacific, Gibraltar), insulation installers (TopBuild, IBP).
ideas.mechanism: Hail of 1.5 inches or larger damages roofs; insurers pay for replacement and re-roofing follows one to nine months later, pulling shingle, underlayment, siding, gutter and insulation volumes through distributors. A hail index = sum over storm days of (NEXRAD MESH hail-signature cells or SPC public reports at or above a size threshold) weighted by housing units in the affected 0.1-degree tile (Census) and lagged one to two quarters nowcasts the storm-driven share of roofing volumes in the reporting quarter (REASONED). TESTED HERE: SPC daily hail CSVs return lat/lon/size per report and NCEI SWDI nx3hail returns counts per day, per bounding box and per 0.1-degree tile (1,764 hail-signature cells nationally on 2025-06-15).
ideas.target: revenue and margin (roofing volumes and price/mix)
ideas.measurement_window: Hail days in the reporting quarter and the two prior quarters (weighted toward the prior one to two quarters); data is near-real-time so the final reading is available at quarter end, ~4 weeks before Owens Corning reports.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1%: about 8-12 names: OC (~$12B), CSL (~$15B, mostly commercial roofing so weaker), QXO (roofing distribution after the Beacon acquisition, REASONED), ROCK (~$1.5B), LPX (~$6B), BLD (~$10B), IBP (~$5B), JELD, NX; caps REASONED.

ideas.who_already_knows: Everyone knows storms matter: OC and Beacon discuss 'storm demand' qualitatively each quarter and sell-side reads ARMA shingle shipment statistics, which are quarterly and typically published after OC reports (REASONED). Verisk and CoreLogic sell hail-exposure and roof-claim analytics mainly to insurers (REASONED). A quantified hail-exposure times rooftop-density index tied to the building-products print is uncommon in sell-side work (REASONED), so the sign is priced but the magnitude is not.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Verisk, CoreLogic (hail and claims analytics for insurers; REASONED). None of the brief's listed alt-data vendors.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Free, daily, radar-derived swaths weighted by rooftop density and lagged to the re-roofing cycle, aimed at a building-products revenue surprise rather than insurer losses.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A one-standard-deviation positive anomaly in the rooftop-weighted hail index over the trailing two quarters, measured 5 trading days before the release, predicts a positive roofing-volume/revenue surprise and positive T-1 to T+2 abnormal return vs XLI for shingle makers and roofing distributors, controlling for consensus revisions, housing starts, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Roughly four-fifths of asphalt-shingle demand is replacement, and the replacement cycle is pulled forward by hail and wind events that trigger insurance claims (REASONED). Because insurers settle and roofers work through backlogs over months, a spring hail season shows up in second- and third-quarter shipments and pricing.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Storm demand is the most-discussed swing factor in roofing and is partly captured by distributor commentary mid-quarter; asphalt cost pass-through and pricing often matter more than volume; public hail reports are biased toward populated areas, double-counting density; claim settlement and roofer labour constraints spread demand unpredictably; roofing is only a part of OC's and none of several names' EBIT.
ideas.canonical_name: Rooftop-weighted hail-swath index

vet.changes_made: (1) Make NCEI SWDI nx3hail (radar MESH) tile counts the primary instrument and use SPC public reports only as a cross-check, because public reports are population-biased and would double-count density once housing-unit weighting is applied. (2) Weight 0.1-degree tiles by ACS housing units (Census key). (3) Lag structure: index over the trailing two to three quarters excluding the current month, since claims-to-reroof lags run one to nine months; the reporting quarter's own hail mostly informs guidance, not the quarter. (4) Names: OC and QXO (post-Beacon) primary, CSL secondary; drop BLD, IBP, JELD and NX (insulation/windows have a weak hail link); ROCK optional. (5) Backtest from 2008 (SWDI counts for June 2008 returned 70,931, so history exists) against OC roofing-segment volumes and T-1 to T+2 returns, with controls for the prior-year hail base (storm comps), asphalt cost and housing starts. (6) Crowdedness lowered to 2: storm demand is the most-discussed swing factor and sell-side surveys already cite hail/wind reports.
vet.revised_hypothesis: A one-standard-deviation positive anomaly in the housing-unit-weighted NEXRAD MESH hail index over the trailing two to three quarters (excluding the current month), measured 5 trading days before the release, predicts a positive roofing-volume/revenue surprise and positive T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus XLI for OC and QXO (CSL secondary), controlling for the prior-year hail base, consensus revisions, asphalt cost, housing starts, sector, size and momentum.
vet.revised_universe_coverage: ~0.3%: OC, QXO primary; CSL secondary; ROCK optional.

ideas.name: Sunbelt pool-permit counts from city and county open-data portals as a new-pool-construction nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Pool and irrigation: pool shells (Latham), pool equipment (Hayward), pool distribution (Pool Corp), with irrigation permits as a side read for Toro.
ideas.mechanism: Every in-ground pool needs a building permit, and large Sunbelt cities publish issued permits daily on Socrata or ArcGIS portals with description, sub-type and issue date. Weekly counts of pool permits across FL/TX/AZ/CA metros nowcast new-pool starts, which drive essentially all of Latham's volume (fiberglass and vinyl shells ship at dig stage, REASONED) and the new-construction share of Hayward's and Pool Corp's sales (roughly 20-25%, REASONED). Permits lead installation by two to eight weeks, so the quarter's permits map to the same and following quarter's revenue. TESTED HERE: Austin's permit dataset returns ~160-310 permits per month with 'POOL' in the description for 2024-2026, and Los Angeles' building-permit dataset returns ~250-390 per month.
ideas.measurement_window: Permits issued during the fiscal quarter plus the preceding four weeks; portals update daily, so the final reading is available at quarter end, three to six weeks before SWIM/HAYW/POOL report.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.4%: 3-5 names: HAYW (~$3B), POOL (~$10-12B), SWIM (~$0.7B, borderline on dollar volume), TTC (~$8B, irrigation side read); LESL likely below the size floor; Fluidra foreign. Caps REASONED.

ideas.sector_focus: Specialty vehicles and municipal machinery: REV Group, Oshkosh (Pierce, McNeilus), Federal Signal (Elgin, Vactor), Blue Bird, Alamo Group, Douglas Dynamics, Miller Industries.

ideas.name: FracFocus job-level disclosures: pumper, proppant and water volumes by supplier as an oilfield-services nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Pressure pumping, frac sand, produced/sourced water logistics, completion chemicals.
ideas.mechanism: Every hydraulically fractured well in the major producing states must be disclosed on the FracFocus registry with job start and end dates, operator, total base water volume and an ingredient list in which each ingredient carries a supplier name (often the pressure pumper or the proppant/chemical supplier) and mass. Counting jobs and summing proppant mass and water volume by supplier per week nowcasts completions revenue for pumpers and tons or barrels for sand and water names. Texas ties the disclosure to the completion report, due within about 30 days of completion (16 TAC 3.29; REASONED), other states allow up to 60 days (REASONED), so an as-of-date backfill curve must be modeled.
ideas.measurement_window: At 5 days before earnings (about 30-40 days after quarter end), months 1-2 of the quarter are near-complete and month 3 is roughly half reported; the point-in-time estimate must be corrected with the historical reporting-lag curve.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1.5%: about 15-20 names. Liberty Energy (LBRT), ProPetro (PUMP), ProFrac (ACDC), Patterson-UTI (PTEN, includes NexTier), Atlas Energy Solutions (AESI, proppant), Select Water Solutions (WTTR), Aris Water (ARIS), Innospec (IOSP, oilfield chemicals segment), Solaris Energy Infrastructure (SEI), Core Lab (CLB), Cactus (WHD, less direct).

ideas.who_already_knows: Primary Vision's weekly frac spread count is widely circulated, and Enverus and Rystad sell completions datasets built partly from FracFocus, so crew-count activity is largely priced (REASONED). The narrower slice, supplier-attributed proppant tons and water barrels and per-job intensities, is less commonly built, and small-cap sand/water names get thin coverage.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: Enverus, Rystad Energy, Primary Vision (frac spread count).
ideas.why_ours_differs: Supplier-attributed volumes (proppant tons for Atlas, water barrels for Select/Aris, job counts per pumper) instead of crew counts; free; explicit as-of backfill modeling for a point-in-time estimate.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A change of at least 10% in FracFocus-attributed proppant mass (sand names) or job count (pumpers) over months 1-2 of the quarter versus the same months of the prior quarter, measured 5 days before earnings and adjusted for the reporting-lag curve, predicts the sign of the revenue surprise and the close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus OIH, controlling for consensus revisions, the quarter's WTI change, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Completions, not drilling, drive revenue for pumpers, sand and water companies, and activity swings within quarters as operators exhaust or extend budgets. Each frac job consumes thousands of tons of sand and hundreds of thousands of barrels of water, so job-level disclosures sum to supplier volumes.

ideas.name: Sentinel-2 stockpile footprint and ship presence at Core's Baltimore terminal and Warrior's Mobile pad as an export-shipment nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Coal producers with owned or dedicated export terminals (met and thermal export).
ideas.mechanism: Core Natural Resources owns the CONSOL Marine Terminal in Baltimore (Curtis Bay), the export outlet for its Pennsylvania Mining Complex and Leer met coal, and Warrior Met Coal ships essentially all output through the McDuffie terminal in Mobile. Sentinel-2 (10 m, 5-day revisit) resolves the stockpile pad area and bulk carriers at berth; pad-area change plus berth-occupancy days over a quarter nowcasts terminal throughput (shipments) versus mine output (inventory build or draw). Exporters recognize revenue on shipment, not production, so quarterly shipments can diverge materially from steady output. TESTED HERE: Planetary Computer STAC returned 6 Sentinel-2 L2A scenes with under 30% cloud over Curtis Bay between 1 October and 10 November 2026.
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter; last clear scene typically within 5 days of quarter end; processing is immediate; earnings follow 30-45 days after quarter end.
ideas.universe_coverage: <1%: Core Natural Resources (CNR), Warrior Met Coal (HCC); partial for Alpha Metallurgical (AMR) and Core via the shared NS Lamberts Point pier. Extendable (REASONED) to single-company ore docks (Cliffs Silver Bay) and Gulf petcoke/sulfur terminals.

ideas.name: BLS PPI detailed-commodity indexes as full-quarter realized-price nowcasts for single-product chemicals, metals and packaging names
ideas.sector_focus: Chlor-alkali and PVC, TiO2, carbon black, nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers, aluminum and steel products, glass containers, paperboard.
ideas.mechanism: Monthly PPI commodity indexes are built from transaction prices (contract and spot) that producers report for the week of the 13th; the month-3 index is released around the 13th-16th of the following month, before most Q3 materials earnings in late October to early November, so the full-quarter average realized-price proxy is known one to three weeks before results. For single-product producers (chlorine/caustic to Olin, PVC to Westlake, TiO2 to Kronos/Tronox/Chemours, carbon black to Cabot/Orion, nitrogen to CF/CVR Partners/LSB, aluminum sheet to Kaiser/Constellium, glass containers to O-I, paperboard to Graphic Packaging/Sonoco), quarter-average PPI change times guided volume approximates revenue change; the gap versus consensus revenue, which analysts build from spot assessments, is the signal.
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter (three monthly PPI readings) as of roughly day 13-16 of the month after quarter end; initial PPI values are revised for four months.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~8%: roughly 100 names across chemicals, metals, packaging and fertilizers, e.g., OLN, WLK, KRO, TROX, CC, CBT, OEC, CF, UAN, LXU, MOS, KALU, CSTM, CENX, OI, GPK, SON, SLGN, CLF, CMC, ATI, CRS, HWKN, ASIX, MTX, IOSP, AVNT. Mapping of each name to its dominant 6- to 8-digit PPI commodity code is the setup work.

data_sources.name: BLS Public Data API v1 (keyless, ~3 years) / v2 (free registration key, 20 years, 500 queries per day); example series WPU10 (metals and metal products); detailed chlor-alkali, TiO2, fertilizer, container and paperboard codes to be looked up in the PPI commodity database (REASONED)
data_sources.update_frequency: monthly, released about day 13-16 of the following month
data_sources.history_depth: many commodity codes 1947+ or 1980s+ (REASONED); v1 keyless returns ~3 years

data_sources.name: BLS PPI commodity data finder (series lookup; not tested)

ideas.cost: $0 (free BLS v2 key).
ideas.who_already_knows: PPI is a mainstream macro release, and chemical and metals analysts prefer ICIS, S&P Global Commodity Insights, Argus and Fastmarkets weekly spot assessments (paid), which lead PPI; the specific test of quarter-average detailed PPI against consensus revenue is not standard (REASONED). Priced-in share is high for spot-driven products and lower for contract-heavy ones (TiO2, caustic, cans, paperboard) where PPI captures contract resets.
ideas.vendors_selling_similar: ICIS, S&P Global Commodity Insights (IHS Markit), Argus, Fastmarkets sell price assessments; nobody sells PPI, which is public.
ideas.why_ours_differs: Transaction-weighted, includes contract pricing, free, full-quarter reading before earnings, and covers about 100 names at once; the measured quantity is the realized-price level, not the price-change frequency of the seed item.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A deviation of at least 3% between the quarter-average detailed PPI for a company's dominant product (segment-revenue weighted) and the price path implied by consensus revenue (consensus quarterly revenue change minus guided volume change), measured 10 days before earnings, predicts the sign of the revenue surprise and the close T-1 to close T+2 abnormal return versus XLB, controlling for consensus revisions, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Commodity chemical, metal and packaging producers have little quarter-to-quarter pricing power, so realized price times volume is revenue and price drops fall to margin with a lag. Producers themselves report transaction prices to BLS, so the index reflects actual contract resets rather than only spot quotes.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: PPI is sampled, sometimes imputed and revised for four months, and may lag spot by a month; many 'single-product' names are mixed by product and region (TiO2 is global); consensus already embeds spot moves that lead PPI; and the PPI release moves the whole sector so the idiosyncratic residual may be small.
ideas.seed_item_extended: [digital] Price-change frequency in B2B and industrial-distributor catalogs

ideas.name: FMCSA roadside-inspection count per carrier USDOT number as a monthly fleet-activity and safety-cost nowcast
ideas.sector_focus: Asset-based truckload and LTL carriers, owner-operator networks, dedicated and drayage fleets
ideas.mechanism: State and federal enforcement generate roadside inspections roughly in proportion to a carrier's highway exposure (tractor-miles, weigh-station passes), so the monthly number of inspections tagged to a carrier's USDOT number tracks its active tractor count and miles driven, which is the volume driver of truckload revenue (loaded miles x rate per mile) and LTL linehaul activity. A carrier parking trucks, losing drivers or shrinking its fleet shows fewer inspections in the same month; one growing a dedicated fleet or absorbing an acquisition shows more. Driver and vehicle out-of-service rates from the same records move with driver tenure and deferred maintenance, which feed claims/insurance and maintenance expense, a margin item carriers rarely guide. TESTED HERE: Werner (DOT 53467) ~370-630 inspections/month, Knight (428823) ~240-340, Marten (74432) ~170-340, Saia (29124) ~130-200, Heartland (134697) ~90-170, with data through 2026-11-08 in a file refreshed 2026-11-10.
ideas.target: revenue (miles, tractor count); margin (out-of-service and violation rates feeding insurance and maintenance)
ideas.measurement_window: Calendar quarter, daily inspection records. Months 1-2 are complete well before earnings; month 3 is ~70-90% complete at T-14 because states upload within ~21 days (REASONED from SMS methodology), so use a vintage-adjusted month 3 or months 1-2 only.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2%: about 20-25 names. Truckload WERN, HTLD, MRTN, KNX, SNDR, CVLG, PTSI, ULH; LTL SAIA, ARCB, XPO (ODFL is above the cap); owner-operator network LSTR (Landstar Ranger/Inway DOT numbers); intermodal/drayage fleets HUBG, JBHT; dedicated lessor R. ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: A decline of at least 8% in quarter-to-date inspections per MCS-150 power unit versus the same quarter a year earlier (deflated by the national inspection count trend), measured 14 days before the earnings release, predicts a negative revenue surprise and a negative T-1 to T+2 abnormal return versus IYT for asset-based carriers, controlling for consensus revisions over the prior 30 days, sector, size and momentum.
ideas.industry_context: Truckload carriers earn revenue per loaded mile, so the number of active tractors and miles driven in the quarter is most of the volume story, yet carriers only disclose fleet size quarterly. Every commercial truck on US highways is subject to roadside inspection, and each inspection is logged against the carrier's USDOT number in a public federal database.
ideas.strongest_reason_wrong: Inspection intensity is targeted: the Inspection Selection System sends more inspections to carriers with worse safety scores, so counts can rise while miles fall (TESTED HERE: Werner's monthly count rose from ~450 in 2025 to ~600 in 2026; whether that is miles or targeting is UNKNOWN until checked against reported tractor counts). ideas.name: Gulf Coast unplanned petrochemical outage hours (TCEQ and LDEQ emission-event reports) as a nowcast of inland tank-barge and tank-car demand
ideas.sector_focus: Inland tank-barge operators; chemical railcar lessors
ideas.mechanism: Kirby's inland fleet moves petrochemicals, refined products and black oil between Texas and Louisiana plants, and management routinely attributes weak quarters to customer plant outages and navigation delays (REASONED from company commentary). Texas rules require operators to report unplanned emission events within 24 hours to TCEQ, whose public database lists facility, start and end time, cause and type; Louisiana's LDEQ holds the equivalent. Summing event-hours at the largest barge-served crackers, refineries and chemical sites, weighted by their liquid-cargo relevance, gives a near-real-time count of lost liftings, which drives barge utilization and spot rates within the quarter; chemical tank-car utilization for GATX and Trinity follows more weakly. TESTED HERE: a POST search returned events through 2026-11-10 including Lubrizol Deer Park, INEOS Chocolate Bayou and LyondellBasell Bayport; the database runs from 2003-01-31; an RSS feed of recent events is offered.
ideas.target: revenue and margin (barge utilization, spot rates) for KEX inland marine; guidance
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter of event-hours (events posted within 1-2 days of start); KEX reports ~4 weeks after quarter end.

ideas.name: FAA aircraft-registry nightly diffs: delivery, sale-leaseback and retirement timing for US airlines and lessors
ideas.sector_focus: US airlines taking deliveries; aircraft and engine lessors with US-registered assets
ideas.mechanism: The FAA publishes every US-registered aircraft's record nightly (N-number, serial, model, registrant, certificate issue date, status). A new registration of an airline's serial number marks a delivery; a registrant change to a bank trustee marks a sale-leaseback closing; a cancellation marks a retirement or export sale. Delivery timing within the quarter drives capex, capacity and ownership cost, and sale-leaseback gains are a recurring reported EPS item for Frontier and Sun Country (REASONED from their filings). For lessors with US-registered fleets, registrant transfers reveal trades before the quarterly letter. Applies to US-registered operators; most of Air Lease's fleet is foreign-registered and not covered.
ideas.target: capex; EPS surprise (gain on sale-leaseback); guidance (capacity)
ideas.measurement_window: Quarter-to-date registrations, transfers and cancellations by serial number, final at quarter end; forward view from reserved N-numbers pending delivery.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~1.5%: ALK, JBLU, ALGT, SNCY, ULCC, SKYW; lessors WLFC (partial), FTAI (engines not registered), AL (minor US exposure); about 8-10 names (market caps approximate, REASONED).

ideas.name: Fab-cluster equipment trade flows: HS 8486 semiconductor-equipment exports from the US/Japan and imports into Taiwan/Korea/China as a destination-weighted nowcast for mid-cap semi-cap revenue
ideas.sector_focus: Semiconductor equipment and sub-systems
ideas.mechanism: Semi-cap tools are large serialized capital goods that cross a border and are declared under HS heading 8486 (machines for semiconductor and flat-panel manufacture) and 8486.90 (parts). Official customs statistics publish those flows by partner country monthly: Taiwan MOF about 8 days after month end, Korea (KITA/customs) about 15 days, Japan MOF about 20-30 days, US Census about 35-40 days. Mid-cap US equipment makers concentrate in one process step and disclose geographic revenue in XBRL, so a destination-weighted index of HS 8486 flows (US exports to China for Axcelis, Onto, Veeco; flows into Taiwan/Korea for FormFactor, Cohu, Kulicke & Soffa, Ichor, Ultra Clean) nowcasts revenue recognized on shipment or acceptance. ACM Research ships from Shanghai so it is not captured by US exports but is by China imports from Taiwan/Japan of competing tools. Labels: Census endpoint TESTED HERE (returns Missing Key without a key); Taiwan/Korea/Japan portals TESTED HERE for page load only; data queries REASONED.
ideas.measurement_window: Honest coverage: US Census and Japan data give months 1-2 of the quarter before most late-Oct/early-Nov prints (month 3 arrives ~5 weeks after quarter end, often after the print). Taiwan imports give all three months by about the 8th of the month after quarter end (20-30 days lead); Korea by about the 15th (15-25 days). The 14-day figure is for the two-month US/Japan reading.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~2-3%: about 25-35 names in semiconductor equipment and sub-systems. Examples: Axcelis (ACLS), Onto Innovation (ONTO), Veeco (VECO), FormFactor (FORM), Cohu (COHU), Kulicke & Soffa (KLIC), Ichor (ICHR), Ultra Clean (UCTT), Camtek (CAMT).

ideas.sector_focus: Ad-tech (supply-side platforms, intermediaries, native and app monetization)

ideas.name: FedRAMP Marketplace status transitions and reusing-agency counts, paired with FPDS awards, as a federal-bookings lead for SaaS and cybersecurity vendors
ideas.sector_focus: Application and infrastructure software, cybersecurity with federal exposure
ideas.mechanism: Federal agencies may only deploy cloud services that hold a FedRAMP authorization (or are In Process with an agency sponsor). GSA's public FedRAMP Marketplace lists each cloud service offering, its status (In Process, Authorized), impact level (Low/Moderate/High), authorization date and the agencies that have issued or reused the authorization. Federal buying concentrates in the fiscal fourth quarter (July-September), so marketplace changes in the preceding 90 days, combined with FPDS award records naming the vendor (posted within days of award), nowcast and lead federal revenue. ideas.name: Daily gTLD zone-file counts via ICANN CZDS as a near-exact nowcast of registry and registrar domain bases (Verisign, GoDaddy, Wix)
ideas.sector_focus: Internet infrastructure: domain registries, registrars, website builders
ideas.mechanism: ICANN requires gTLD registries to provide daily zone files through the Centralized Zone Data Service to approved users. A zone file lists every delegated domain with its nameservers. Counting .com and .net domains daily nowcasts Verisign's domain name base, whose revenue is essentially base times a fixed, contract-set price, with net adds and renewal rate the only real quarterly variables. Counting domains whose NS records point to a registrar or builder's nameservers (GoDaddy's domaincontrol.com, Wix's wixdns.net, Tucows/Hover) nowcasts those companies' domain and site counts. Net adds equal new names minus deletions, both observable day by day. Labels: CZDS listed as KEY in the working file; NS-share mapping REASONED; Verisign market cap roughly $25-28B so inside the band (REASONED, verify).
ideas.measurement_window: Full quarter of daily counts; the quarter-end base is known one day after quarter end, about 20 days before Verisign's print and 25-35 days before GoDaddy's and Wix's.
ideas.universe_coverage: ~0.3%: 3-4 names. Examples: Verisign (VRSN), GoDaddy (GDDY), Wix (WIX); Tucows (TCX) likely below the cap floor.
